pages.title: Before you read: in their time
sections: Essay

At school, I had a history teacher who began the school year in an unusual way. In the first lesson, he taught no dates, no kings, and no battles. For two hours, he talked instead about how people of the past saw the world: what they feared, what they took for granted, what they could not even imagine. Historians call this the history of mentalities. His point was simple. You cannot understand what people did until you understand the world they did it in.

The same is true of ideas. A sentence written two thousand years ago can feel as if it was written for you this morning. Some ideas really are like that: Seneca's warning that we waste our lives, not that life is short, needs no footnote. Others only show their full weight once you know what surrounded them.

When Epicurus opened his school in Athens, he welcomed women as students, in a city where women were kept out of public life. Today that sounds ordinary; then, it was a quiet revolution. When Socrates kept asking Athenians what they really meant by justice or courage, he was not playing a game. In 399 BCE, a jury sentenced him to death.

It works the other way too. Aristotle, one of the sharpest minds who ever lived, argued that some people are slaves by nature. To him, that was common sense. To us, it is plainly wrong. Knowing his world does not excuse it, but it helps us see how a brilliant person can share the blind spots of his time, and it invites a harder question: which of our own certainties will look like that one day?

Some ideas changed our world precisely because they shocked theirs. Mary Wollstonecraft's claim that women seem weaker only because they are denied an education was radical in 1792. The fact that it sounds obvious now is, in part, her doing.

So as you read the thinkers in this Library, try asking two questions. What did this mean to the people who first heard it? And what does it mean to me, here, today? "In their time" is here to help with the first. The second is yours.

pages.title: Ancient Greece
sections: In one line
Small, proud cities where a few free men argued about everything, and most people had no say at all.
How people lived

Greece was not one country but hundreds of city-states, each with its own laws, gods, and army. Athens, the best known, became a democracy around 508 BCE: citizens voted directly in an assembly. It was also a city at war for much of this time. In 404 BCE it lost a long war against Sparta, and a harsh regime of thirty oligarchs briefly took power.

After Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, the cities lost their independence to large kingdoms. Athens was defeated in 322 BCE, and Macedonian soldiers held its port. This is the world Epicurus taught in, from around 306 BCE: a city that could no longer steer its own fate.
What they believed

Greek religion had no holy book, no single priesthood, and no creed. It was something you did more than something you believed: sacrifices at altars, libations of wine, and festivals, which filled some 140 days of the Athenian year. People consulted oracles, above all the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, and most imagined the dead as spirits in an underworld.

Religion was bound up with the city itself. That is why, in 399 BCE, Socrates was charged with failing to honour the city's gods and with corrupting the young. A jury of about 500 citizens found him guilty, 280 to 221, and sentenced him to death.
Who counted, and who was left out

Only adult male citizens could vote. Athenian women had no legal standing of their own: a father, then a husband, acted for them, and girls often married around fourteen, to men twice their age. Religious festivals were almost the only public life open to them. Foreign residents, called metics, paid a special tax and could neither vote nor own land.

And Athens ran on slavery. There may have been some 80,000 slaves in the city in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, and most free families owned at least one. The worst work was in the silver mines. Few Greeks questioned this. Aristotle called slaves "living tools"; one of the rare dissenters, the orator Alcidamas, answered that "nature has made nobody a slave".
Ahead of their time

Most Athenians took the gods, customs, and values of their city as given. Socrates kept asking what those ideas really meant, and in 399 BCE the city put him to death for it.

In most Greek cities, women were kept out of public life and learning. Epicurus welcomed women into his school. Most Greeks honoured the gods through public rites. Heraclitus mocked some of those rites openly.
What still echoes today

The word "democracy", the habit of asking for reasons, and the question of how to live a good life all come from these cities. So does a warning: Aristotle's claim that some people are slaves by nature was used, centuries later, to defend the enslavement of Native Americans.

pages.title: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
header: Lucretius, Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Boethius
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: In one line
A huge empire that brought peace to the Mediterranean for two centuries, run on slave labour, where philosophy became a practical guide for living well under powers you could not control.
How people lived

In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus, and he became the first emperor. The roughly 200 years that followed are known as the Roman Peace. At its height, the empire held perhaps 55 to 60 million people, between a sixth and a quarter of everyone alive.

People spoke Latin in the West and Greek in the East. Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch were the largest cities, each about twice the size of any European city in the early 1600s. Trade routes grew fast in the first two centuries CE.
What they believed

Romans worshipped many gods, and later also their emperors. Then Christianity spread. In 313 Constantine gave Christians the right to worship openly, in 380 Theodosius made Christianity the state religion, and in 391 he closed the old temples.

Among the educated, Stoicism was a guide to daily life. It taught that you control only your own judgements and choices, and that the rest is not yours to command. That message spoke both to a man born a slave and to an emperor.
Who counted, and who was left out

Rome was a slave society. Slaves came from war, piracy, kidnapping, and birth. Caesar alone sold 53,000 people from one tribe. By law a slave was property, with no right to sue or make contracts. Many were freed, and some freedmen grew rich, but their own path to high office stayed closed.

Women were citizens but could not vote or hold office. They could own property, make wills, and divorce, and many upper-class women were well educated. In 212 CE, citizenship was extended to all free people in the empire.
Ahead of their time

Romans treated a slave as property, not a person. Epictetus, born a slave around 50 CE, taught the opposite: no one can own your judgements and choices, so freedom does not depend on your legal status.

Roman society ranked people sharply by birth and status. Yet the emperor Marcus Aurelius drew on the teaching of this former slave in his own thinking.
What still echoes today

In 476 the last Western emperor was forced to step down. Some fifty years later, Boethius, a senior official under the Gothic king Theodoric, was arrested for treason and executed in 524. In prison he wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy*.

The question these thinkers kept asking is still ours: how do you stay steady when events, bosses, and luck are not in your hands?
sources: Wikipedia, "Christianity as the Roman state religion"

pages.title: China of the Hundred Schools
sections: In one line
Centuries of war between rival states, when rulers hired wandering thinkers to tell them how to bring back order, and China produced more schools of thought than at almost any other time.
How people lived

The Zhou kings had once ruled over many lords. After their court moved east in 771 BCE, their power faded, and a few strong states swallowed the weaker ones. From about 475 to 221 BCE, the Warring States period, war never really stopped.

War grew in size. Iron weapons replaced bronze, and armies of chariots gave way to masses of foot soldiers with swords and crossbows. Battles could last months. Some states built the first real bureaucracies, run by officials chosen for their work rather than their birth.
What they believed

Since the Zhou, people believed Heaven gave the right to rule to a virtuous king, and could take it back from a bad one. The big question of the age was practical: how do you end the chaos? Every school had its answer.

Confucius (551–479 BCE) said order begins with good people in right relationships. Mozi argued for equal care for all and against wars of attack. The Daoist texts linked to Laozi advised living with the grain of nature and ruling by doing less. The Legalists said people are selfish, so only strict laws and punishments work.
Who counted, and who was left out

Society was strongly patriarchal. The ideal was "men plough, women weave", and a woman's place was inside the home. Girls from about age ten were taught to obey father, then husband, then sons. Daughters were often seen as worth less than sons.

The records still show women advising rulers, judging guests, and writing poetry. One Zhou king even named his wife among his nine ministers. Most of what we know concerns noble families. The lives of ordinary farmers left few traces.
Ahead of their time

Under the Zhou, land and power passed down through noble families. In this era, a teacher with no title could travel from court to court and win a post as an adviser on government, war, or diplomacy. Some states began to choose officials for their work, not their family.

Kings claimed to rule with Heaven's favour. Mencius, one of the boldest thinkers of his age, turned this around. He ranked the people first and the ruler last, and said a ruler who harms the state should be replaced.
What still echoes today

In 221 BCE the state of Qin conquered the others, and its king declared himself the first emperor. In 213 BCE the Qin ordered many books burned, including writings of the Hundred Schools. Historians still argue about how much was really lost.

The Han dynasty that followed blended Confucian and Legalist ideas into a system of government that lasted, in its main lines, until the late 19th century. Questions about merit, duty, and good leadership from these schools are still part of how millions of people think about work and family.
sources: Wikipedia, "Burning of books and burying of scholars"
Wikipedia, "Women in ancient and imperial China"

pages.title: Ancient India
header: The Upanishads, the Dhammapada, the Bhagavad Gita, the Questions of King Milinda
sections: In one line
An age of forest teachers, wandering monks, and royal debates, when India asked who we really are beneath our roles, and how to act well in a world of endless rebirth.
A word on dates

Dates in this era are uncertain, often by centuries. These texts were spoken and memorised long before they were written down, and many grew over time. Scholars place the oldest Upanishads around the 7th to 6th century BCE, and the Bhagavad Gita anywhere from the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. We give ranges, not exact years.
How people lived

In the Ganges plain, kingdoms grew, and kings held court with learned priests. One famous Upanishad describes a contest of ten sages at the court of King Janaka, debating the nature of reality before the king.

Alongside the priests lived the *shramanas*, people who left home and family to seek truth as wandering ascetics. Several such movements already existed by the 6th century BCE. The Buddha and the Jain teacher Mahavira came from this world in the 5th century BCE.
What they believed

The Vedas, old hymns and rituals kept by priests, were the core of religious life. The Upanishads turned inward. They taught that *Atman*, the inner self, and *Brahman*, the reality behind everything, are one and the same.

Ideas of karma and rebirth took shape in this period, perhaps first among the ascetics. Many shramana groups rejected the authority of the Vedas and their rituals.
Who counted, and who was left out

An old hymn describes society in four classes: priests, rulers and warriors, farmers and merchants, and labourers and servants. Scholars see this, in early times, more as an ideal than a fixed reality. People outside the four classes were treated as outcastes.

Women appear in the debates, if rarely. Gargi questions the sage Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court, and his wife Maitreyi asks him what makes a person immortal. They are the exception in texts written and kept by men.
Ahead of their time

In a society organised by class, many held that birth is what makes a person a priest. Early Buddhist texts disagreed. In one dialogue, a priest is led to agree that what truly counts is virtue and wisdom, not birth.

Many seekers of the time believed the spiritual life meant leaving home and family behind. The Bhagavad Gita offered another way. Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna to do his duty in the world, but without craving the results. Action itself can be a spiritual path.
What still echoes today

In the 2nd century BCE, Indo-Greek kings ruled in the north-west. The *Questions of King Milinda* records, or imagines, a long dialogue between one of them, Menander, and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. It is an early meeting of two worlds, built on patient questions.

The Gita's advice to act fully while letting go of the outcome still speaks to anyone who works hard for results they cannot control.

pages.title: The medieval Islamic world
header: Omar Khayyam, al-Ghazali, Ibn Arabi, Rumi, Sa'di, Hafiz
sections: In one line

A world of great cities, schools, and libraries, broken by the Mongol invasions, where scholars weighed reason against faith and poets turned the love of God into some of the most loved verse ever written.
How people lived

By the 11th century, Baghdad had been a centre of learning for centuries. Scholars there had translated Plato, Aristotle, Galen, and Ptolemy from Greek into Arabic. Paper, which came from China in the 8th century, made books cheaper and easier to spread.

Power had passed to Turkish rulers, the Seljuks. Their vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded a network of colleges, the first in Baghdad in 1065. Omar Khayyam, born in Nishapur in 1048, worked for the Seljuk sultan, building an observatory and reforming the Persian calendar. He was also a serious mathematician, who developed the first general theory of cubic equations.
What they believed

Islam shaped law, learning, and daily life. Within it, two paths met and sometimes clashed: the jurists, who studied the law, and the Sufis, who sought closeness to God through love, prayer, and the remembrance of God.

From the 12th century, Sufi brotherhoods formed and spread across the Muslim world. Persian poets such as Rumi, Sa'di, and Hafiz gave this inner search its most famous voice.
Who counted, and who was left out

The colleges were open only to men. Women from leading city families were often taught at home, and many earned certificates in religious studies, calligraphy, or poetry. Some women worked as physicians in hospitals.

Slavery was part of life, including in the army. *Mamluks* were boys bought, often from Turkic lands, converted, and trained as soldiers. Freed as adults, they formed a ruling class, and from 1250 they ruled Egypt and Syria themselves.
Ahead of their time

The jurists, who studied the law, and the Sufis, who sought God through love, were often at odds. Al-Ghazali, a professor at the great college in Baghdad, refused to choose. He brought law and Sufi practice together, and helped Sufism spread.

To many readers, the language of wine and drunkenness had no place in religion. Sufi poets such as Hafiz used it anyway, as an image of the love of God. Some critics doubted whether this was still Islam.
What still echoes today

In 1219 the Mongols invaded. They destroyed great cities such as Merv, Nishapur, and Herat. In 1258 they took Baghdad, killed the caliph, and massacred its people, an event often seen as the end of the Golden Age of Islamic learning.

Yet much of the poetry was written in or after these years of loss. Rumi's and Hafiz's verses are still read, quoted, and sung today, far beyond the Muslim world.
sources: Wikipedia, "Mongol conquest of Persia and Mesopotamia"

pages.title: Japan, from the Heian court to the age of the samurai
header: Sei Shōnagon, Kamo no Chōmei, Kenkō
pages.era: Japan, from the Heian court to the age of the samurai
sections: In one line
A refined court that prized beauty, a country slowly taken over by warriors, and a Buddhism that believed the world was in decline.
How people lived

In 794 the emperor moved his capital to Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, and gave the age its name. Over time, real power passed to a great noble family, the Fujiwara. The court was tiny: perhaps 5,000 aristocrats in a land of some five million people. In that small world, beauty was seen as part of what made a person good.

Outside the capital, a new class of provincial warriors, the samurai, grew stronger. A civil war between two warrior clans ended in 1185, and the victor, Minamoto no Yoritomo, set up a military government at Kamakura. The court survived, but the warriors ruled. They held off two Mongol invasions, in 1274 and 1281, before their own regime fell in 1333.
What they believed

Many Japanese Buddhists believed they lived in *mappō*, the age of decline of the Buddha's teaching, which by their count began around 1052. This belief helped give rise to new schools of Buddhism in the Kamakura years, such as the Pure Land school of Hōnen and the school of Nichiren. Zen also took root, brought by Eisai and Dōgen.

Disaster was never far away. In *Hōjōki*, Chōmei describes a great fire in 1177, a whirlwind and a forced move of the capital in 1180, and a famine in which one monk counted 42,300 bodies in the capital alone.
Who counted, and who was left out

The literature of this age was written by and for a tiny elite, a few thousand people in a land of millions. Within it, women were mostly kept from Chinese learning, the prestige writing of men. But they wrote in Japanese, in a script called "women's hand", and much of the great writing in Japanese came from court women.
Ahead of their time

Women at court were kept from Chinese learning, the writing that carried the most prestige. Sei Shōnagon wrote in Japanese instead, and filled her book with her own opinions, likes, and dislikes, with unusual freedom.

People who turned away from the world usually went to live in a temple. Chōmei took Buddhist vows in 1204, but chose another path: he built a tiny hut in the hills outside the capital and lived there alone. In *Hōjōki* he set down his life in the hut, after the disasters he had seen.
What still echoes today
Kenkō's question still speaks to us: should we look at the moon only when it is full, or at flowers only in full bloom? These writers taught that things can be beautiful because they pass.

pages.title: Renaissance Europe
header: Petrarch, Erasmus, Machiavelli, Montaigne, Francis Bacon
sections: In one line
After the plague, Europe went back to the books of Greece and Rome to find a better way to live, and found itself questioning the Church, the prince, and its own customs.
How people lived

The Black Death reached Europe in 1347. In a few years it killed perhaps 30 to 60 percent of the population, by different estimates. Workers became scarce and wages rose. The old order of lords and peasants began to loosen.

Italy was a patchwork of rich, rival city-states. Florence, where the Renaissance began, was run by merchant families such as the Medici, who paid artists like Leonardo and Michelangelo. From about 1440, printing spread from one shop in Mainz to some 270 cities. By 1500, more than 20 million books had been printed.
What they believed

Nearly everyone was Christian, and the Church shaped every part of life. The humanists did not reject faith. They wanted to go back to the sources: ancient texts read in their original languages, for lessons in how to live and speak well.

Petrarch (1304–1374) hunted through old libraries for lost Latin works by Cicero and Seneca. Erasmus, the most printed author of the early 1500s, published the New Testament in Greek in 1516. He wanted the Church reformed from within and stayed Catholic all his life.
Who counted, and who was left out

When the plague came, Jews were falsely accused of poisoning wells. In 1349 about 2,000 were murdered in Strasbourg alone, and by 1351 hundreds of Jewish communities had been destroyed. Many fled east to Poland.

Women rarely appear in the record of the age. A few broke through, like the painter Sofonisba Anguissola. After 1492, Europeans also met the peoples of the Americas for the first time.
Ahead of their time

Europeans took it for granted that their own world was the civilised one. Montaigne wrote about the Tupinambá of Brazil, who ate their dead enemies, and compared their customs with the cruelty of Europe in his own day. He judged both by the same standard.

Writers on government usually told princes how a good ruler should behave. Machiavelli lost his post when the Medici returned to Florence in 1512, and was imprisoned and tortured. In 1513 he drafted *The Prince*, which looked instead at how rulers really gain and keep power.
What still echoes today

In 1517 Luther challenged the Pope, and Europe split. In France, wars between Catholics and Protestants ran from 1562 to 1598 and cost perhaps 2 to 4 million lives. In 1572, thousands of Protestants were killed in the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre.

Montaigne lived through all of it. He withdrew to his tower in 1571 to write his *Essays*, then served as mayor of Bordeaux, respected by both sides. His habit of doubting his own certainty is the era's most useful gift.
sources: Encyclopædia Britannica, "Black Death: effects and significance"
Encyclopædia Britannica, "Michel de Montaigne: the Essays"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Michel de Montaigne"

pages.title: Europe in the 17th century
header: Descartes, Hobbes, Pascal, Spinoza, Locke, La Rochefoucauld, La Bruyère
sections: In one line
A century of religious war, revolution, and new science, when thinkers looked for a certainty that no church or king could guarantee anymore.
How people lived

From 1618 to 1648, the Thirty Years' War tore through central Europe. It started as a fight between Catholics and Protestants and became a contest of crowns. Historians disagree on the toll, but millions died, most of them from plague, hunger, and disease. Some German regions lost more than half their people.

England had its own civil wars. In 1649 Parliament executed King Charles I, and the country became a republic for a time. The king returned in 1660, and in 1688 another king was pushed out in favour of a monarchy limited by Parliament.
What they believed

Christianity was still the frame of life, but there were now several churches, each sure it was right. Living next to people of another faith was a new and dangerous problem. The Dutch Republic tolerated many faiths, as long as they were practised quietly.

At the same time, a new science was reading nature in the language of mathematics. In 1633 the Church found Galileo strongly suspect of heresy for teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun. He had to reject his views and spent the rest of his life under house arrest.
Who counted, and who was left out

Few women had a public voice in philosophy, but some entered the debate by letter. From 1643, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes until his death. Her first question went to the heart of his system: how can a mind that has no body move a body?

The new ideas of freedom had blind spots. Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Yet he also invested for a time in a company that traded enslaved Africans, and helped draft a colonial constitution that gave free men total power over their slaves. Historians still debate how large his role was.
Ahead of their time

Most of Europe was ruled by kings with near-total power. In *Leviathan* (1651), Hobbes still defended a strong ruler, but on new grounds: people agree to obey one power to escape the horror of civil war. Locke went further, arguing that government rests on the consent of the governed.

Communities expected their members to share their faith. Spinoza did not, and in 1656, at 23, the Jewish community of Amsterdam expelled him for heresy. He made his living grinding lenses, published his political treatise in 1670 under a false name and place, and left most of his work to be printed after his death.
What still echoes today

Two questions from this century are still open. How do you know what you know, when authorities disagree? And what do rulers owe the people they rule?

The French moralists of the time, La Rochefoucauld and La Bruyère, asked a third, more personal one: how much of what we call virtue is really self-interest in disguise?
sources: Encyclopædia Britannica, "Germany: the Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Elisabeth of Bohemia"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Locke's Political Philosophy"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy"

pages.title: The Enlightenment
header: Voltaire, Émilie du Châtelet, Hume, Adam Smith, Rousseau, Diderot, Vauvenargues, Kant, Chamfort, Mary Wollstonecraft
sections: In one line
The century that told people to think for themselves and put reason, rights, and freedom at the centre of public life, while leaving out much of humanity.
How people lived

Most Europeans still lived under kings. Some rulers, such as Frederick the Great of Prussia and Catherine the Great of Russia, took up new ideas and called themselves enlightened. Ideas travelled through salons, coffeehouses, scientific academies, and a fast-growing world of print.

In Paris, elite women such as Madame Geoffrin hosted salons where writers met to argue. From 1751 to 1772, Diderot and d'Alembert, with about 150 others, published the *Encyclopédie*, 35 volumes meant to gather all human knowledge.
What they believed

Christianity was still the official faith almost everywhere, but many writers questioned the power of churches. Their faith was in reason and in evidence. Kant summed up the spirit of the age in two Latin words, *sapere aude*: dare to know.

Thinking freely had a price. In France, writers fought the censors and were sometimes jailed or forced into exile. Voltaire spent time in the Bastille twice, and one of his books was publicly burned. Many banned books were printed in the Dutch Republic and smuggled into France.
Who counted, and who was left out

The age of rights was also an age of the Atlantic slave trade. Over the centuries of that trade, between 10 and 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships to the Americas, and up to two million died on the crossing. Many countries that embraced the new ideas excluded slavery from them.

Women were rarely treated as equals in these debates. Émilie du Châtelet was once thrown out of a Paris café where scholars met, and came back dressed as a man.
Ahead of their time

Women could attend the Academy of Sciences in Paris only as listeners. Yet in 1739, Émilie du Châtelet's essay on fire became the first work by a woman the Academy published. Her French translation of Newton, finished in 1749, the year she died, is still the standard one.

Many writers, Rousseau among them, held that women should obey men. Mary Wollstonecraft disagreed. In 1792, in *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, she argued that women, given a real education, would be thinking people and better citizens, and should have civil and political rights of their own.
What still echoes today

The ideas of the age helped inspire the American and French Revolutions. In 1791, enslaved people in Haiti rose up. Their revolt forced revolutionary France to abolish slavery in 1794, and showed that the rights of man had to be claimed by those left out of them.

Human rights, free speech, and a free press are still argued in the language this century created. So is the question of who gets left out of "everyone".
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Émilie Du Châtelet"

pages.title: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
header: Schopenhauer, John Stuart Mill, George Eliot, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Nietzsche
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: In one line
Factories, revolutions, and new science shook the old certainties, and thinkers asked what a person should live by once faith, rank, and tradition no longer held.
How people lived

In Britain, large numbers of people left the land for the factory towns. Before 1833, some cotton mills ran up to 71 hours a week, and children often started work at four or five. Crowded, dirty housing helped spread cholera and typhoid. Laws slowly capped working hours and banned young children from the mines.

In 1848, revolutions broke out in more than fifty countries. People demanded a voice in government, a free press, and rights for workers. Most of the uprisings were crushed, but some reforms lasted, such as the end of serfdom in Austria and Hungary.

In Russia, the tsar feared the revolutions would spread. In 1849 the young Dostoevsky was arrested for taking part in a circle that discussed banned books. He and the others were led out to be shot and pardoned only at the last moment, in a scene staged on the tsar's orders. He spent the next years in prison and exile.
What they believed

Most Europeans were still Christian, but faith was under pressure. In 1859 Darwin published *On the Origin of Species*, which argued that living things evolve through natural selection. It clashed with the belief that each species was designed and fixed.

In 1882 Nietzsche wrote that "God is dead". He did not mean a being had died. He meant that belief in the Christian God, which had long given Europe its morals and meaning, was fading, and that people had not yet faced what that would mean.
Who counted, and who was left out

In Russia, millions of peasants were serfs, bound to the land and to their masters. In 1861 the tsar freed more than 23 million of them. Most then had to pay for their land over 49 years.

Women had few legal rights, and no vote. Mary Ann Evans published her novels as George Eliot, in part so they would be judged on their merits and not as "women's writing".
Ahead of their time

The law gave husbands power over their wives, and most people saw this as the natural order. In 1869, in *The Subjection of Women*, Mill called it wrong and argued for full equality between the sexes. He even compared the position of married women under the law to slavery.

Living with a man outside marriage broke the rules of Victorian society. The writer George Henry Lewes could not divorce his wife under English law, so George Eliot lived with him openly, as his wife in all but name, from 1854 until his death in 1878. It shocked many, and her own brother cut her off. She refused to hide it.
What still echoes today

The great questions of this century were moral ones. If the old rules no longer hold, what should we live by? Dostoevsky and Tolstoy looked for an answer in faith and conscience, Mill in freedom and fairness, and Nietzsche in the courage to create new values.

We still live with their questions, in a world of fast change, fading traditions, and choices that are more and more our own.
sources: Wikipedia, "Life in Great Britain during the Industrial Revolution"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "John Stuart Mill's Moral and Political Philosophy"

pages.title: America in the 19th century
header: Emerson, Margaret Fuller, Thoreau, Emily Dickinson, William James
sections: In one line
A young country that preached freedom while holding millions in slavery, where a small circle of New England writers told people to trust their own conscience over custom and the crowd.
How people lived

The United States grew fast and pushed west. Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, somewhere between 60,000 and 100,000 Native Americans were forced from their lands in the South-East. About 15,000 of them died on the way, on what became known as the Trail of Tears.

In 1860 about four million people were enslaved, nearly one American in eight. The country went to war with itself from 1861 to 1865. Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865.
What they believed

Most Americans were Protestant Christians. In 1836, near Boston, Emerson and a few friends began meeting to discuss what they found lacking in the churches and colleges of their day. Critics called them "Transcendentalists", and the name stuck.

Emerson's essay *Nature*, published that same year, became their manifesto. Their message, in short: look for truth in your own experience and in nature, not only in books and pulpits.
Who counted, and who was left out

Women could not vote, and few had a public voice.

In 1848, about 300 people met at Seneca Falls, New York, for the first women's rights convention. The call for women's right to vote was the most debated resolution. Frederick Douglass, the only African American present, spoke in favour.
Ahead of their time

The law of the land allowed slavery and backed a war of conquest against Mexico. Thoreau argued that a person's conscience can outrank the law. In 1846 he refused to pay a tax that might help fund a war he opposed and a system that allowed slavery, and spent a night in jail. His essay on it, now known as *Civil Disobedience*, later inspired Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

Women were expected to keep to the home. Margaret Fuller edited the Transcendentalists' journal, *The Dial*, and in 1845 published *Woman in the Nineteenth Century*, which urged women to seek independence through education and work. It is often called the first major feminist book in the United States.
What still echoes today

These writers asked how a person keeps their integrity inside a society they disagree with. Thoreau's answer was quiet refusal. Fuller's was to speak up in public.

Emily Dickinson's answer was a private world of words. She wrote nearly 1,800 poems, but only ten were published in her lifetime, altered to fit the taste of the day. The rest were collected only after her death, from 1890.

Their ideas about self-reliance, nature, and conscience shaped American culture, and the question they raised is still with us: when should you follow the rules, and when should you follow your own judgement?
sources: Wikipedia, "End of slavery in the United States"

pages.title: Asia meets the West
sections: In one line
As Western empires and Western ideas pressed on Asia, three thinkers spoke to the West in its own language, and asked it to listen as well as teach.
How people lived

India was ruled by Britain. Famine struck again and again. About 15 million people died in major famines between 1850 and 1899, and at least 5.6 million in the Great Famine of 1876–1878 alone.

Japan took another path. In 1853 American warships arrived and forced it to open its ports, and soon after it had to accept unequal trade treaties. In 1868 a new government took power in the emperor's name. It abolished the samurai class, built schools, factories, and an army, and borrowed Western science under the slogan "rich country, strong army".
What they believed

India and Japan faced the same question: what to take from the West, and what to keep. Japan's new public schools taught lessons shaped by the European Enlightenment, alongside Western science and technology.

The three thinkers of this era answered by bringing Asian ideas to the West. Vivekananda taught Vedanta and yoga to Western audiences. Tagore translated his own poems into English. Okakura wrote *The Book of Tea* in English in 1906, linking the way of tea to Japanese life and art, and pushing back against Western clichés about "the East".
Who counted, and who was left out

Under colonial rule, Indians had little say in how their own country was run. Tagore openly called for independence from Britain.

In 1913 Tagore became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. In 1919, after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar, he gave back his British knighthood.
Ahead of their time

Many in the West saw Asian cultures as backward, and judged a nation by its strength at war. Okakura turned this around in *The Book of Tea*: the West called Japan barbarous while it practised the gentle arts of peace, and civilised only once it won a bloody war in Manchuria.

For many Indians, nationalism was the road to freedom. Tagore wanted independence too, but he was critical of nationalism and the walls it builds between countries. In his novel *Ghare Baire* (The Home and the World), he set a calm reformer against a fiery nationalist leader.
What still echoes today

These three did not reject the West. They wrote and spoke in English and went to meet Western audiences. But each pushed back against the idea that Asia had only things to learn.

On 11 September 1893, at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago, Vivekananda greeted the audience as his sisters and brothers. About 7,000 people gave him a standing ovation.

The question these three left is still open: how do you stay rooted in your own culture while staying open to the world?
sources: Encyclopædia Britannica, "The Home and the World"

pages.title: Europe in the age of world wars
pages.era: Europe in the age of world wars
sections: In one line
Thirty years of total war, mass murder, and broken faith in progress, when philosophers asked what a human life is worth and what we owe one another.
Why only one thinker here

This era produced many of the thinkers people know best today, among them Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, and Camus. Their works are still protected by copyright, so the app cannot yet share their words the way it shares older texts. Simone Weil stands here alone for that reason, not because she was the only voice of her time. We will add others as their works enter the public domain.
How people lived

The First World War, from 1914 to 1918, killed somewhere between 15 and 22 million people, soldiers and civilians. France alone lost about 1.7 million, more than 4 percent of its population.

The peace did not last. The Second World War killed somewhere between 60 and 85 million people, about 3 percent of everyone alive in 1940.
What they believed

After the slaughter of 1914–1918, the belief that the world was steadily getting better was hard to hold. People looked for meaning in politics, in faith, or in neither.

Simone Weil, born in Paris in 1909 to a secular Jewish family, tried more than one of these paths. She studied philosophy at the École Normale Supérieure, taught, and was a pacifist until the rise of the Nazis changed her mind.
Who counted, and who was left out

Between 1941 and 1945, Nazi Germany and its allies murdered around six million Jews, about two-thirds of the Jews of Europe. Millions of others were also persecuted and killed. In 1942 Weil left France with her family for the United States, then went to London to work for the Free French.

Women in France did not gain the right to vote until 1944, and first voted in 1945. Until 1965, a married Frenchwoman needed her husband's consent to take a job.
Ahead of their time

Few philosophers had seen factory work from the inside. In 1934, Weil took a year off teaching to work, unknown, on factory assembly lines, including at Renault, to learn what that labour does to a person. In 1936 she went to Spain to join an anarchist unit in the civil war, until an accident forced her home.

Since the French Revolution, European politics had been built on the language of rights. Weil argued that obligations come first: a right means something only when others do their duty to respect it. In 1943, as de Gaulle's Free French drafted a new declaration of the rights of man, she wrote a draft statement of human obligations instead, and set out her view in *The Need for Roots*.
What still echoes today

Weil died in England in 1943, aged 34, of heart failure, while ill with tuberculosis and eating no more than she believed people in occupied France were given. Almost all her major works were published only after her death. Her questions about attention, the dignity of work, and the need for roots are still ours.

The questions of this era sit under much of today's thinking about human rights, about work, and about how ordinary people can be drawn into great evil.

pages.title: Buddhist Philosophy
sections: In one line
The Buddha's teachings read as a practical philosophy: an ethics and a training of the mind to end suffering.
Where and when

The Buddha, born Gautama in Lumbini, in today's Nepal, taught in northern India, most likely in the 5th century BCE. His teaching began as one of several movements of wandering seekers, then spread across Asia along the Silk Road, and reached the West in the 19th century.

Today it is both a religion, followed by hundreds of millions of people, and a philosophy studied by many who do not practise it. The app reads it mainly as philosophy, through two texts: the *Dhammapada*, a collection of 423 short verses in 26 chapters, and *The Questions of King Milinda*, a dialogue between a Buddhist monk and a Greek king of north-west India.
Key ideas

- **Life is marked by *dukkha*:** suffering, or the unease of relying on things that do not last.
- **Everything changes,** yet we crave and cling to what cannot stay.
- **No fixed self:** there is no permanent, unchanging soul behind our thoughts and feelings.
- **Actions have consequences** (karma): what we do shapes who we become.
- **The Middle Way** between harsh self-denial and indulgence, through ethics, meditation, and wisdom.
Who we read
The Buddha (the *Dhammapada*) and *The Questions of King Milinda*.
Next to its neighbours

Buddhism grew in the same soil as Indian Philosophy and shares ideas such as karma and rebirth. But it parts ways on the self: where the Upanishads look for a deep, lasting self, Buddhism denies there is one. Its focus on calming the mind also echoes the Stoics and Epicureans, a few centuries later and a long way west.
Where to start reading
The *Dhammapada*: short verses that can be read one at a time, in any order.

pages.title: Classical Greek Philosophy
sections: In one line
Where Western philosophy began: asking what the world is made of, and then how we should live.
Where and when

Greek philosophy began in the 6th century BCE in the cities of the eastern Aegean, with thinkers who swapped myths for reasoned explanations. Around 500 BCE, Heraclitus of Ephesus saw the world as constant change.

In Athens, Socrates (about 470–399 BCE) turned philosophy towards ethics. He wrote nothing and was sentenced to death by an Athenian court. His student Plato founded the Academy, and Plato's student Aristotle founded the Lyceum and taught the young Alexander the Great. From there, a clear line runs to Roman, Islamic, medieval, Renaissance, and Enlightenment thought.
Key ideas

- **Change is everywhere** (Heraclitus): "everything flows", yet a hidden order, the logos, holds it together.
- **Question everything,** including yourself (Socrates): his method of short questions and answers still bears his name.
- **Beyond what we see** (Plato): the changing world is an imperfect copy of perfect, unchanging Forms.
- **Character is built by practice** (Aristotle): we become good by doing good things, until they become habits.
- **The goal is flourishing** (*eudaimonia*): a whole life lived well, not a passing feeling.
Who we read
Heraclitus, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.
Next to its neighbours

The Stoics and the Epicureans grew out of this world, after Aristotle. Both took the classical question, how to live well, and turned it into a daily practice with a single clear answer: virtue for the Stoics, pleasure as calm for the Epicureans. The classical thinkers argued more and settled less. They also lived in a society built on slavery, and Aristotle argued that some people are slaves by nature.
Where to start reading
Plato, *Apology*: Socrates' defence speech at his trial. It is short, and it shows why he chose death over silence.
sources: The app's thought #109 (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II)

pages.title: Confucianism
sections: In one line
A Chinese tradition built on good character, learning, and harmony in families and society.
Where and when

Confucius (about 551–479 BCE) was born near Qufu, in the small state of Lu, in eastern China. He saw himself not as an inventor but as a transmitter of older values that his age had lost. He taught thousands of students, and his sayings were collected by his followers in the *Analects*, many years after his death.

Mencius developed his ideas a century later. Suppressed under the harsh Qin dynasty, Confucianism became China's official philosophy under the Han, around 130 BCE. For centuries it was the basis of the exams that chose government officials, until they were abolished in 1905.
Key ideas

- **Humaneness** (*ren*): kindness and care for others, the heart of a good person.
- **Ritual and good manners** (*li*): the forms that make respect visible, from greetings to funerals.
- **The "superior person"** (*junzi*): noble by character, not by birth.
- **Family duty:** respect for parents, the root of a good society.
- **Lead by example:** a ruler who acts rightly will be followed without force.
Who we read
Confucius and his students, and Mencius.
Next to its neighbours

Where Taoists step back from society, Confucians step into it, and try to make it better through learning and duty. The tradition also built rules that bound women. From the Han period on, Confucian teachers taught that a virtuous woman should follow her father, then her husband, then her sons. Early 20th-century Chinese reformers blamed Confucianism for China's troubles, but interest in it has returned since.
Where to start reading
Confucius, *Analects*: short sayings and exchanges with his students. Open it anywhere.

pages.title: Enlightenment Ethics
sections: In one line
The age that put reason, evidence, and freedom at the centre of how we live and govern ourselves.
Where and when

The Enlightenment grew out of the scientific revolution of Galileo and Newton. It took shape in Western Europe in the 17th century; one common starting point is Descartes' *Discourse on Method* (1637).

It peaked in the 18th century, in salons, coffeehouses, academies, and a booming world of print. Its great project was the French *Encyclopédie* (1751–1772), edited by Diderot and d'Alembert. Historians usually end the period with the French Revolution in 1789, or at the latest with Kant's death in 1804. Our path stretches a little further, to Mill in the 1860s.
Key ideas

- **Think for yourself:** test beliefs by reason and evidence, not by tradition alone.
- **Why we need government** (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau): power rests on an agreement among the people, not on birth.
- **Freedom and tolerance:** of religion, of speech, of how you live.
- **Morality from feeling or from duty:** Hume and Adam Smith start from sympathy; Kant from duty; Mill from the greatest happiness.
- **Women's minds** (du Châtelet, Wollstonecraft): women are rational beings and deserve the same education.
Who we read
Descartes, Hobbes, Spinoza, Locke, Hume, Voltaire, Émilie du Châtelet, Adam Smith, Rousseau, Diderot, Kant, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Mill.
Next to its neighbours

The Humanists before them looked back to ancient wisdom; the Enlightenment looked forward, to progress. Its ideals also had clear limits. Many European colonies ran on slave labour, and even Locke, who called freedom a natural right, allowed slavery for captives taken in a just war. In 1791, enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, in what became the Haitian Revolution.
Where to start reading
Mill, *On Liberty* (1859): the case for free thought and free living, still argued over today.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Positive and Negative Liberty"

pages.title: Epicureanism
sections: In one line
A philosophy of quiet happiness: simple pleasures, good friends, and a mind free from fear.
Where and when

Epicurus founded the school in Athens in 307 BCE. It met in his garden, so it became known simply as "the Garden", and it welcomed women among its students. In the 1st century BCE, the Roman poet Lucretius set out its ideas in a long poem, *On the Nature of Things*.

The school was a rival first of Plato's followers, then of the Stoics. It declined as Christianity spread; Dante even placed the Epicureans in hell. Later thinkers rediscovered it, and Thomas Jefferson called himself an Epicurean.
Key ideas

- **Pleasure is the goal of life,** but the pleasure that counts is the absence of pain in the body and of fear in the mind.
- **Desire less.** Some desires are natural and easy to meet; others, like the hunger for wealth and power, can never be satisfied.
- **Death is nothing to fear:** when it is here, we are not.
- **The world is made of atoms and empty space.** The gods, if they exist, do not interfere in human life.
- **Friendship** is the greatest help to a happy life.
Who we read
Epicurus and Lucretius.
Next to its neighbours

The word "epicurean" now suggests fine food and luxury. That is close to the opposite of what Epicurus taught: he and his friends were known for simple meals and long conversations. Next to the Stoics, the Epicureans also sought a calm mind, but through pleasure rather than virtue, and by keeping out of politics rather than serving the city.
Where to start reading
Epicurus, *Letter to Menoeceus*: a few pages that hold the whole philosophy. Then the *Principal Doctrines*, a list of short sayings.

pages.title: Existential Thought
sections: In one line
Writers who faced life's hardest questions head-on: freedom, suffering, meaning, and how to live with them.
Where and when

The word "existentialism" only appeared in the mid-20th century, with Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Camus. These best-known existentialists are still under copyright, so the app reads the writers who came before or alongside them.

The questions are older. Pascal, a French mathematician, asked them in the 1650s. In the 19th century, Schopenhauer, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, and Nietzsche pushed back against neat systems that explained everything except how to live. In America, William James asked what makes life worth living, and Simone Weil, who died in 1943, brings the path into the 20th century.
Key ideas

- **Life comes before theory:** start from real human experience, not abstract systems.
- **Freedom is a gift and a weight.** We have to choose, and we carry the responsibility.
- **Anxiety is part of being free:** the dizziness of having to decide.
- **Meaning is not handed to us;** we have to find it, or make it.
- **Authenticity:** live your own life, not the one others expect.
Who we read
Pascal, Schopenhauer, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Nietzsche, William James, and Simone Weil.
Next to its neighbours

The Enlightenment trusted reason to improve the world. These writers doubted that reason alone could tell a person how to live. Some, like Pascal, Tolstoy, and Weil, answered through religious faith; others, like Schopenhauer and Nietzsche, did not. Nietzsche's work was later bent out of shape: after his death, his sister edited his writings to fit her nationalist views, and the Nazis claimed him, although he had openly opposed antisemitism and nationalism.
Where to start reading
Dostoevsky, *Notes from Underground*: a short novel, angry and funny, about a man who refuses to be reasonable.

pages.title: Humanists and Essayists
sections: In one line
Writers who explored how to live in personal prose, short sayings, and poems, rather than in grand systems.
Where and when

The path spans five centuries. It begins in Renaissance Italy in the 1340s with Petrarch, called the father of humanism, who collected and taught the ancient Greek and Roman writers. Humanism then spread north with printing, to Erasmus and beyond, while Machiavelli took a hard look at power as it is, not as it should be.

In France, Montaigne invented the essay in 1580, from the French *essayer*, "to try"; in England, Francis Bacon wrote the first essays in English in 1597. Then came the French moralists, La Rochefoucauld, La Bruyère, Vauvenargues, and Chamfort, masters of the short, sharp maxim.

From 1836, in New England, Emerson, Thoreau, and Margaret Fuller belonged to the Transcendentalist circle, which trusted intuition, nature, and self-reliance. Emily Dickinson and George Eliot share their spirit.
Key ideas

- **Learn from the ancients,** then think for yourself.
- **Write from your own life:** Montaigne made himself the subject of his own book.
- **Say it short:** a maxim should surprise you into seeing something true.
- **Look at people as they are,** vanity and self-interest included.
- **Trust yourself and nature** over custom and crowds.
Who we read
Petrarch, Erasmus, Machiavelli, Montaigne, Francis Bacon, La Rochefoucauld, La Bruyère, Vauvenargues, Chamfort, Emerson, Margaret Fuller, Thoreau, Emily Dickinson, and George Eliot.
Next to its neighbours

The Stoics and Confucians tell you how to live. These writers mostly show you how they lived, or how people really behave, and let you draw the lesson. Some readers find the moralists cynical, and Machiavelli has given his name to ruthless politics. Read them as observers, not as role models.
Where to start reading
Thoreau, *Walden*: two years in a cabin by a pond, and what he learned about needing less.

pages.title: Indian Philosophy
sections: In one line
Philosophy from India's Hindu tradition, asking what our deepest self is, and how to act well in the world.
Where and when

It begins with the Upanishads, Sanskrit texts composed between about 800 and 300 BCE. They moved away from the rituals of the older Vedas towards meditation and questions about consciousness. The *Bhagavad Gita*, likely composed in the 2nd or 1st century BCE, is a 700-verse dialogue within the great epic, the *Mahabharata*.

Later, six classical schools took shape; one of them, Vedanta, became the most influential. In modern times, Swami Vivekananda brought Vedanta to the West, with a famous speech in Chicago in 1893. In 1913, the poet Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize.
Key ideas

- **Atman and Brahman:** the deepest self (Atman) is one with ultimate reality (Brahman), at least in the Vedanta school.
- **Act without clinging to results:** do your duty (*dharma*), but let go of the fruits of your actions.
- **Many paths:** through action, knowledge, and devotion.
- **Karma and rebirth:** actions shape what follows, in this life and beyond.
- **Liberation** (*moksha*): freedom from that cycle, through self-knowledge.
Who we read
The Upanishads, the *Bhagavad Gita*, Vivekananda, and Tagore.
Next to its neighbours

Buddhism shares karma and rebirth with this path but denies a lasting self, while the Upanishads put that self at the centre. The *Gita* also has a hard setting: on a battlefield, the god Krishna, in Hindu tradition, persuades the warrior Arjuna to fight. Readers have taken it very differently since. Gandhi learned verses from its second chapter by heart and treated them as a companion for his non-violent struggle.
Where to start reading
The *Bhagavad Gita*: short chapters, each on one question about how to act.

pages.title: Japanese Aesthetics
sections: In one line
Finding beauty in what is simple, imperfect, and passing, and paying full attention to small moments.
Where and when

The path covers nine centuries of Japanese writing. Around 1000 CE, Sei Shōnagon, a lady at the imperial court in Kyoto, wrote *The Pillow Book*: lists, scenes, and sharp opinions about what is beautiful and what is not.

In 1212, Kamo no Chōmei, a court poet who had lived through fires, famine, and an earthquake in Kyoto, left society for a tiny hut in the mountains and wrote *An Account of a Ten-Foot-Square Hut*. In the early 14th century, the Buddhist monk Kenkō wrote *Essays in Idleness*, still one of the most studied works of medieval Japanese literature.

In 1906, Okakura Kakuzō wrote *The Book of Tea* in English, to explain Japanese culture to Western readers who often caricatured it.
Key ideas

- **Mono no aware,** "the pathos of things": a gentle sadness at how everything passes, which makes it more beautiful.
- **Wabi:** the beauty of what is plain and stark.
- **Sabi:** the beauty of age and wear, like moss on stone.
- **Yūgen:** deep, quiet grace that is felt more than seen.
- **Simplicity** in daily life, as in the tea ceremony.
Who we read
Sei Shōnagon, Kamo no Chōmei, Kenkō, and Okakura Kakuzō.
Next to its neighbours

These ideals grew from Shinto's love of nature and Buddhism's teaching that all things are impermanent, with Taoist and Zen influences as well. Where the Buddhists see impermanence as a source of suffering to overcome, these writers often find it a source of beauty to enjoy.
Where to start reading
Okakura, *The Book of Tea*: short, written in English, and a door into the whole path.

pages.title: Persian and Sufi Poetry
sections: In one line
Wisdom poetry from the Persian-speaking world and from Sufism, on love, longing, the present moment, and how to treat one another.
Where and when

The path runs from the 11th to the 14th century, across Persia and the wider Islamic world. It opens with Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) of Nishapur, a mathematician and astronomer who designed a calendar still at the root of the Persian one; short four-line poems attributed to him question fate and celebrate the present. Al-Ghazali (about 1058–1111), a leading scholar in Baghdad, gave up his post after a personal crisis in 1095 and turned to the Sufi path.

Ibn Arabi (1165–1240), born in Murcia, in today's Spain, taught that all things are expressions of one single reality. Rumi (1207–1273) settled in Konya, in today's Turkey; his long poem, the *Masnavi*, is among the greatest in Persian. Sa'di (about 1210–1291) and Hafiz (about 1325–1390) both came from Shiraz, and many Persian speakers still know Hafiz's poems by heart.
Key ideas

- **Love** as the deepest force in a life, often love of God, sometimes of a person, and often both at once.
- **Seize the day** (Khayyam): life is short and uncertain.
- **We are one family:** Sa'di's lines on all people as parts of one body hang on a carpet in the United Nations building.
- **Teach through stories,** as in Sa'di's *Gulistan*.
- **The inner path:** purify the heart and let go of the ego.
Who we read
Omar Khayyam, Sa'di, Rumi, Hafiz, al-Ghazali, and Ibn Arabi.
Next to its neighbours

Sufism is the spiritual and mystical tradition within Islam, centred on love of God and remembrance of Him. Khayyam was not a Sufi, which is why the path has its wider name. In the West, these poets are often read through free translations: Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version of Khayyam made him famous in English, but it is free, close to a paraphrase in places.
Where to start reading
Sa'di, *Gulistan* (*The Rose Garden*): short stories with a lesson, in prose and verse.

pages.title: Stoicism
sections: In one line
A practical philosophy for living well: train your judgments, act with virtue, and accept calmly what you cannot control.
Where and when

Zeno of Citium founded the school in Athens around 300 BCE. He taught in the Stoa Poikile, a painted colonnade on the main square, which gave the school its name. Chrysippus, its third head, turned it into a full system of logic, physics, and ethics.

Stoicism then spread across the Greek and Roman world and lasted until the 3rd century CE. Its best-known voices are Roman: Seneca, a statesman; Epictetus, a teacher; and Marcus Aurelius, an emperor. It faded after Christianity became Rome's state religion, then came back in the Renaissance and again today.
Key ideas

- **Virtue is the only good.** Health, wealth, and pleasure have value, but they do not make a life good or bad.
- **Some things are up to us, others are not.** Our judgments and actions are ours; most of the rest is not.
- **Live in agreement with nature,** which for the Stoics means living by reason.
- **Strong emotions come from false judgments,** so they can be changed by thinking more clearly.
- **Practice daily:** philosophy is a training, not a theory. Seneca, for one, looked back each evening at how he had spent his day.
Who we read
Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Seneca, and Boethius.
Next to its neighbours

Stoics and Epicureans both wanted a calm mind, and both lived in the same city at the same time. They disagreed on the goal. For the Stoics it was virtue; for the Epicureans it was pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and fear. The Stoics also expected you to take part in public life, while the Epicureans mostly stayed out of politics.
Where to start reading
Marcus Aurelius, *Meditations*: private notes, written in short entries that you can open anywhere. Then Epictetus's *Enchiridion*, a short handbook.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Seneca" (on the evening review)

pages.title: Taoism
sections: In one line
A Chinese tradition of living in harmony with the Tao, the natural way of things, through simplicity and effortless action.
Where and when

Taoist thought took shape in China during the Warring States period, between about 450 and 300 BCE. Its two founding texts were compiled then: the *Tao Te Ching*, short poetic chapters traditionally credited to Laozi, and the *Zhuangzi*, full of stories.

Tradition makes Laozi an archivist at the Zhou court and an older contemporary of Confucius; scholars are divided, and some think he is partly or wholly legendary. Taoism later also became an organised religion, with its own priests, rituals, and scriptures. The *Tao Te Ching* is one of the most translated books in the world, second only to the Bible.
Key ideas

- **The Tao** is the way of things: always changing, and impossible to fully put into words.
- **Effortless action** (*wu wei*): act without forcing, like water finding its way around a stone.
- **Naturalness** (*ziran*): let things be what they are.
- **Three treasures:** compassion, humility, and frugality.
- **Softness beats hardness:** the yielding outlasts the rigid.
Who we read
Laozi and Zhuangzi.
Next to its neighbours

Taoism and Confucianism grew up side by side and are often read as a pair. Confucians build a good society through learning, ritual, and duty. Taoists distrust that effort and prefer to step back: fewer rules, less striving, more trust in nature. Both shaped Chinese life for over two thousand years, and many people drew on both.
Where to start reading
Laozi, *Tao Te Ching*: 81 short chapters, best read slowly, one at a time.
sources: The app's thoughts #410, #422, and #425 (Tao Te Ching 8, 43, and 76)

pages.title: Adam Smith
sections: Who he was

Smith was born in Kirkcaldy, a small port in Fife; his father died two months before he was born. He studied in Glasgow and at Oxford, then gave public lectures in Edinburgh that made his name, and became a close friend of the philosopher David Hume.

As professor of moral philosophy in Glasgow, he wrote *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759). Seventeen years later came *The Wealth of Nations* (1776), the book that made him "the father of economics".
What he cared about

The app reads Smith the moral philosopher, not the economist. In his first book he asks how we come to judge right and wrong:

- **Sympathy:** however selfish we are, we care about what happens to others, and feel with them.
- **The impartial spectator:** we judge ourselves by imagining how a fair outside observer would see us.
- **Feelings shape happiness:** love is pleasant in itself, while hatred and anger poison a good mind.
- **No special moral sense:** our judgments of right and wrong grow out of this everyday fellow feeling.
What might surprise you

The thinker best known for self-interest and the market began with a book about kindness and fellow feeling. Many scholars now read his two books as one project, not two opposite views of human nature.

His friends also found him comically absent-minded. He had odd habits of speech and walk, and was known to talk to himself, a habit he had had since childhood.
Where to start reading
*The Theory of Moral Sentiments*, Part I: the opening chapters on sympathy. The original 1759 English is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Adam Smith thoughts (#184–186), from *The Theory of Moral Sentiments*

pages.title: Al-Ghazali
sections: Who he was

Al-Ghazali was born near Tus, in north-eastern Persia, and studied in Nishapur. The powerful vizier of the Seljuk Empire took him under his wing and, in 1091, made him head of the Nizamiyya in Baghdad, the most prestigious teaching post in the Muslim world.

Four years later, at the height of his fame, he went through a deep personal crisis. He gave away his wealth, left Baghdad, and spent years in Damascus, Jerusalem, and Mecca, then in quiet seclusion back home. He returned to teaching only briefly, and died in Tus in 1111.
What he cared about

- **Honest doubt:** in his autobiography, *Deliverance from Error*, he describes testing every source of knowledge until he found certainty.
- **Knowing is not enough:** he realised he had chosen status and ego over the inner life he wrote about.
- **The Sufi path:** purifying the heart through practice, not only through study.
- **Happiness:** knowing yourself is the first step to true happiness, the theme of *The Alchemy of Happiness*.
What might surprise you

He was a gifted philosopher who wrote a famous attack on the philosophers. His *Incoherence of the Philosophers* took aim at thinkers like Avicenna who built on Aristotle and Plato.

Scholars still argue about its effect. Some blame it for a later decline of science in the Islamic world; others say that decline had other causes. His contemporaries gave him the title "Proof of Islam".
Where to start reading
*The Alchemy of Happiness*: his own shorter Persian version of his greatest work. Claud Field's 1909 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's al-Ghazali thoughts (#560–561, #578, #600–602), from *The Confessions* and *The Alchemy of Happiness*

pages.title: Aristotle
sections: Who he was

Aristotle was born in Stagira, in northern Greece. His father was physician to the king of Macedon, which may explain his lifelong interest in biology and medicine. Orphaned young, he was raised by a guardian, and at about eighteen he joined Plato's Academy in Athens, where he stayed for nearly twenty years.

After Plato died, he spent years studying plants and sea creatures on the island of Lesbos. In 343 BCE Philip II of Macedon asked him to tutor his son, the future Alexander the Great. Back in Athens, Aristotle founded his own school, the Lyceum, with a large library.
What he cared about

Aristotle wrote on almost everything, from logic and physics to poetry and politics. On how to live, his main ideas:

- **Flourishing** (*eudaimonia*) is the goal of life: a whole life lived well.
- **We become what we do:** just by doing just acts, brave by doing brave ones.
- **Friendship** at its best is between good people who love each other for who they are.
- **Humans are social by nature;** we flourish only in a community with laws.
- **Good laws** are reason free from passion.
What might surprise you

Only about a third of what he wrote has survived, and none of it was meant for publication. The polished dialogues he wrote for readers are lost; what we read are works he never prepared for the public.

For centuries he was simply "the First Teacher" to Muslim scholars and "the Philosopher" to Christian ones like Thomas Aquinas. Yet he also argued, in his *Politics*, that some people are slaves by nature, a view later used to defend slavery.
Where to start reading
The *Nicomachean Ethics*, Books I and II: what a good life is, and how good character is built. Free online in older translations.
sources: The app's Aristotle thoughts (#109–120, #126–131, #144–151), including #109, #118, and #129

pages.title: Arthur Schopenhauer
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who he was

Schopenhauer was born in Danzig, today's Gdańsk, into a wealthy merchant family, and his inheritance earned him more each year than a professor's salary. He gave up a merchant apprenticeship to study, and published his main work, *The World as Will and Representation*, in 1818.

He tried to teach in Berlin, and scheduled his lectures at the same hour as those of Hegel, the most famous philosopher of the day, whom he called a charlatan. From 1833 he lived alone in Frankfurt, with a series of pet poodles, and recognition came late: in his final years, admirers bought his portrait and visited the places he had lived.
What he cared about

Schopenhauer is known as the philosopher of pessimism. Behind everything, he saw a blind, restless will that keeps us wanting. His ideas:

- **Life swings between pain and boredom;** happiness is mostly the absence of both.
- **What you are inside** matters more for happiness than what you have or what others think of you.
- **Riches and fame are like sea water:** the more you drink, the thirstier you get.
- **Compassion** is the root of morality: we feel another's suffering as our own.
- **Think for yourself:** reading is thinking with someone else's head.
What might surprise you

He was one of the first Western philosophers to take Indian thought seriously. He called the Upanishads the solace of his life, and named one of his poodles Atman, the Sanskrit word for the self.

He also held openly hostile views of women. His 1851 essay "On Women" mocked what he saw as a foolish reverence for women, and it still feeds sexist views today. He later admitted, after meeting the sculptor Elisabet Ney, that he had not yet said his last word on the subject.
Where to start reading
*The Wisdom of Life* and *Counsels and Maxims*: short, practical essays on happiness, far easier than his main work. T. Bailey Saunders's translations are free on Project Gutenberg.

pages.title: Baruch Spinoza
sections: Who he was

Spinoza was born in Amsterdam into a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled to the more tolerant Dutch Republic. He received a traditional Jewish education. In 1656, at 23, the leaders of his community expelled him for his views, with the harshest ban they had ever pronounced.

From then on he belonged to no religious group. He earned his living by grinding lenses and lived quietly in Rijnsburg, Voorburg, and The Hague, surrounded by a small circle of friends. He turned down a chair of philosophy at Heidelberg, perhaps to keep his freedom of thought, and died at 44.
What he cared about

In his *Ethics*, set out like a geometry book, with definitions and proofs, he looks for a calm, free life:

- **God or Nature:** there is only one reality, and it can be called either.
- **Bondage** is being ruled by our emotions; **freedom** is understanding them.
- **Understanding heals:** an emotion loses its grip once we see it clearly.
- **The free person thinks of life,** not of death.
- **Happiness is not the reward of virtue,** but virtue itself.
What might surprise you

His *Theological-Political Treatise* questioned the divine origin of the Bible and argued that religious authorities should have no role in a democratic state. It was banned as blasphemous, and his *Ethics* was published only after his death, by friends.

The lens grinding that fed him may also have helped kill him: he died of a lung disease, probably tuberculosis, possibly made worse by glass dust. Einstein later named him as the philosopher who most shaped his view of the world.
Where to start reading
The *Ethics*, Parts IV and V, on human bondage and freedom. Hard going, but worth it. R. H. M. Elwes's 1883 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Spinoza thoughts (#168–172, #190–191), from the *Ethics*

pages.title: Blaise Pascal
sections: Who he was

Pascal was born in Clermont-Ferrand and lost his mother at three. His father, a tax official, taught him at home. He was a child prodigy: at 16 he wrote an important work on geometry, and at 19 he began building one of the first mechanical calculators.

He went on to shape the theory of probability, in letters with the mathematician Fermat, and to clarify how air pressure and the vacuum work; the unit of pressure is named after him. He was often ill, and died in Paris at 39.
What he cared about

On the night of 23 November 1654, Pascal had an intense religious experience and wrote a short note about it to himself. After that, he turned from science to faith and the human condition. His questions:

- **Our place in the universe:** we are tiny and fragile, yet we can think, and that is our dignity.
- **Distraction:** we keep busy so that we never have to sit alone with ourselves.
- **The limits of reason:** the heart knows things that reason cannot prove.
- **The wager:** a famous argument that, faced with uncertainty, believing in God is the better bet.
What might surprise you

His best-known book is not really a book. The *Pensées* ("Thoughts") are scraps of paper for a defence of Christianity that he never finished, edited by others and published in 1670, eight years after his death. Today they count among the masterpieces of French prose.

He also wrote one of the most quoted apologies in literature. In his *Provincial Letters*, he excused a long letter by saying he had not had time to write a shorter one.
Where to start reading
The *Pensées*: short fragments, some just a sentence, others a page. C. Kegan Paul's 1885 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Pascal thoughts (#225–229), from the *Pensées*

pages.title: Boethius
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: Who he was

Boethius was born in Rome to a noble family, a few years after the last Western Roman emperor was forced from his throne. Italy was now ruled by Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths. Boethius rose fast: senator by 25, consul by 33, and later one of the king's closest advisers.

He also set out to translate the works of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, so that Western readers could study them. In 523 he publicly defended a fellow senator accused of conspiracy and fell from power himself. He was imprisoned in Pavia on a charge of treason and executed in 524.
What he cared about

In prison, he wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy*. In it, Philosophy appears to him as a woman and questions him about his despair. Her lessons:

- **Fortune is a wheel:** it lifts you up and drops you down, and you cannot stop it.
- **Happiness is within,** not in wealth, office, or fame.
- **True friends** are the most precious of riches.
- **Nature needs little,** and very little of that.
- **Nothing is wretched but thinking makes it so.**
What might surprise you

Boethius was one of the leading Christian scholars of his century, yet in the *Consolation* it is Philosophy, not religion, who comes to comfort him. That is one reason the app reads him with the Stoics.

It became one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages. King Alfred translated it into Old English, and Chaucer and Queen Elizabeth I translated it too. He is honoured today as a martyr and saint in Pavia, though some historians doubt that he died for his faith.
Where to start reading
*The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, where Philosophy explains Fortune. H. R. James's 1897 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Boethius thoughts (#28–31, #55–57), from *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II

pages.title: Confucius
sections: Who he was

Confucius, born Kong Qiu, grew up in the small state of Lu, in eastern China. His father died when he was three, and his mother raised him in poverty. He married at nineteen and had a son a year later.

In 501 BCE he became governor of a town, and later Minister of Crime in Lu. Later he left his home state for years, looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice. He came back to Lu at 68 and spent his last years teaching; tradition speaks of three thousand students.
What he cared about

- **Good character,** built through learning and practice, at any age.
- **Do not do to others** what you would not want done to you.
- **Family and ritual:** respect, good manners, and ceremonies hold a society together.
- **Leaders as examples:** a ruler who is upright needs few orders.
- **Learning as joy,** shared with friends.
What might surprise you

Confucius did not see himself as an original thinker. He said he was passing on the wisdom of earlier times, which his own age had forgotten.

One ancient book, the *Xunzi*, tells that soon after becoming Minister of Crime he had a rival scholar executed. Whether this really happened is uncertain, but it sits uneasily with his gentle image. He also rejected violent revolution, even against rulers who had taken power by force.
Where to start reading
The *Analects*: short sayings and conversations with his students, collected after his death. James Legge's 1861 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Confucius thoughts (#467–513), including #467 (Analects 1.1) and #494 (Analects 15.23)

pages.title: David Hume
sections: Who he was

Hume was born in Edinburgh. In his twenties he wrote *A Treatise of Human Nature* (1739–40), an attempt at a science of human nature. It sold so badly that he later said it "fell dead-born from the press". He bounced back, by his own account thanks to a cheerful temper.

His reputation for atheism twice cost him a university chair. He made his name instead as an essayist and historian: his six-volume *History of England* was a bestseller. He worked as a librarian in Edinburgh, then at the British embassy in Paris, and died in Edinburgh in 1776.
What he cared about

Hume wanted to base philosophy on experience, not on ideas we are supposed to be born with. His key points:

- **Reason serves the passions:** our feelings set our goals; reason only finds the way.
- **Habit guides us:** we expect the future to be like the past, though we cannot prove it.
- **Belief should match the evidence,** which made him doubt reports of miracles.
- **Beauty is in the mind** of the one who looks.
- **Stay human:** be a philosopher, but do not forget to live.
What might surprise you

Hume was famous for his good nature and was a close friend of Adam Smith. Yet his kindness to Rousseau, whom he brought to England, ended in a public quarrel, and Hume felt he had to publish his side of the story.

There is also a darker side. In a footnote to his essay "Of National Characters" (1753), he wrote racist claims about non-white peoples. Scholars who admire his work call that note shocking.
Where to start reading
*An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding*: one of the two late works he judged his greatest achievements. Free online.

pages.title: Denis Diderot
tags: Regrets on My Old Dressing Gown
sections: Who he was

Diderot was born in 1713 in Langres, in eastern France, the son of a master cutler. He studied with the Jesuits and thought of becoming a priest, then tried law. When he chose to be a writer instead, his father cut him off, and he lived a poor, bohemian life in Paris for about ten years.
