In 1749 his *Letter on the Blind* made his name and got him jailed for some months at Vincennes. From 1751 he led the *Encyclopédie* with d'Alembert, the great Enlightenment project to gather all human knowledge, including the crafts and trades. Church and state both banned it, and he kept it going for years.

The work left him poor. In 1766 Catherine the Great of Russia bought his library and paid him to look after it for life, and he later spent five months at her court. He died in Paris in 1784.
What he cared about

Diderot was curious about everything, from machines to paintings to the morals of daily life. His themes:

- **The passions:** only strong feeling can raise the soul to great things, though reason must guide it.
- **Knowledge for all:** useful knowledge, from philosophy to the crafts and trades, should be shared.
- **Free thought:** he moved from belief in a distant God towards materialism and atheism.
- **Possessions own us:** buy one fine thing and you soon feel you must replace everything around it.
- **Art seen with fresh eyes:** his reviews of the Paris art exhibitions were among his most admired writing.
What might surprise you

A dressing gown made him famous in economics. In a 1769 essay he describes how a gift of a fine scarlet robe made his old study look shabby, until he had replaced it all and fallen into debt. Today this is called the "Diderot effect".

Much of his best writing stayed in a drawer. *Rameau's Nephew*, *Jacques the Fatalist*, and *The Nun* were published only after his death. In private he was no model of virtue: he was unfaithful to his wife, and his letters to his lover Sophie Volland are among his finest writing.
Where to start reading
"Regrets on My Old Dressing Gown": a few pages, light and very modern. Free online; the app uses its own translations from the French.
sources: The app's Diderot thoughts (#634–635), from *Philosophical Thoughts* and "Regrets on My Old Dressing Gown"

pages.title: Emily Dickinson
sections: Who she was

Dickinson was born in Amherst, Massachusetts, into a prominent family. She studied at Amherst Academy for seven years and spent a short time at Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, then came back home, where she lived most of her life.

She wrote nearly 1,800 poems, but only about ten were published while she was alive. Few people around her knew she wrote at all. After her death, her younger sister Lavinia found the poems in her desk.
What she cared about

Her poems are short, with sharp lines, dashes, and rhymes that do not quite rhyme. Her favourite subjects:

- **Nature,** watched closely, in small details.
- **Death,** a subject she came back to again and again.
- **Kindness:** a life is not wasted if it eases one person's pain.
- **Seeing differently:** what the crowd calls madness can be the deepest sense.
- **Wanting:** we understand success best when we do not have it.
What might surprise you

The first book of her poems, in 1890, was heavily edited to fit the taste of the time. Only in 1955 did a complete edition print the poems close to how she wrote them, dashes and odd capitals included.

Early critics dismissed her as an eccentric recluse who broke the rules of grammar. At least eleven of her poems were dedicated to her sister-in-law, Susan, and some scholars read their bond as a romance.
Where to start reading
*Poems, Series One* (1890): the first selection, short and free online. It is the edited version, so read it knowing some lines were changed.
sources: The app's Dickinson thoughts (#296–298), from *Poems, Series One*

pages.title: Epictetus
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: Who he was

Epictetus was born a slave in Hierapolis, in today's Turkey. He grew up in Rome as the slave of Epaphroditus, a wealthy secretary to the emperor Nero. At some point he became lame: one ancient writer claims his master broke his leg, another that he was disabled from childhood.

He studied Stoic philosophy with Musonius Rufus and, once freed, began to teach. When the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from Rome, Epictetus moved to Nicopolis, in north-west Greece, and opened a school there. He lived simply, with few possessions, until his death.
What he cared about

For Epictetus, philosophy is a way of life, not just a theory. His teaching rests on one idea:

- **Some things are in our power, others are not.** Our judgments, choices, and desires are ours; our body, reputation, and fortune are not.
- **Freedom** is living as we choose, inside what is truly ours.
- **Every event has two handles:** take hold of it by the one you can carry.
- **Responsibility:** we answer for our own actions, through daily self-discipline.
What might surprise you

Epictetus wrote nothing himself. Everything we have comes from his student Arrian, who took down his lessons: the *Discourses* and a short handbook, the *Enchiridion*.

The former slave went on to shape an emperor: Marcus Aurelius was among the many readers he influenced. In old age, the man who lived alone took in a friend's child who would otherwise have been left to die, and raised him.
Where to start reading
The *Enchiridion*: a short handbook, the essence of his teaching in a few pages. George Long's 1877 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Epictetus thoughts (#15–23, #40–46), including #15, #21, and #42

pages.title: Epicurus
sections: Who he was

Epicurus was born on the island of Samos to Athenian parents. Around the age of thirty he began teaching in Mytilene, where his ideas caused enough trouble that he had to leave. He taught next in Lampsacus, then settled in Athens around 306 BCE.

There he bought a garden and founded his school in it. Friends, students, and women lived and studied together and shared their goods. He stayed in Athens for the rest of his life.
What he cared about

Epicurus wanted to free people from the fears that spoil their lives. His main ideas:

- **Pleasure is the goal,** but real pleasure means no pain in the body and no trouble in the mind.
- **Some desires are natural and necessary, others are empty:** wealth and fame never satisfy.
- **Death is nothing to us:** when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not.
- **A wise, honest, and just life** is the only way to live pleasantly.
- **Friends** are the greatest help to a happy life.
What might surprise you

He was said to have written over 300 works, and almost all are lost. What survives is three letters and some short sayings, plus pieces of his great work *On Nature*, found on burnt scrolls in Herculaneum, the town buried by Vesuvius.

He died in great pain from a blocked urinary tract. Yet his last letter to a friend calls it a happy day: against his suffering, he wrote, he set the joy of remembering their conversations.
Where to start reading
The *Letter to Menoeceus*: a few pages that hold his whole view of a good life. R. D. Hicks's 1910 translation is free online.
sources: The app's Epicurus thoughts (#58–73, #77–86), including #59 and #73

pages.title: Erasmus
sections: Who he was

Desiderius Erasmus was born in Rotterdam, probably in 1466 or 1469; even he was unsure. His father was a Catholic priest, so his parents could not marry. Orphaned and poor as a boy, he entered a religious house and was later ordained a priest, though he never had much taste for the monastic life.

He spent his life on the move: Paris, England, Italy, Brabant, Basel, chasing patrons, manuscripts, and printers. In England he befriended Thomas More, and in London, while recovering from illness, he wrote *The Praise of Folly*, which became a best-seller.

In 1516 he published a landmark edition of the New Testament in Greek and Latin. When the Reformation split Europe, he stayed Catholic but argued for reform from within. He died in 1536.
What he cared about

Erasmus was the leading scholar of the Northern Renaissance and wrote in a lively, natural Latin. His themes:

- **Laughing at vanity:** in *The Praise of Folly*, Folly herself mocks self-love and pride.
- **Wisdom at the right moment:** wisdom used out of place is just another kind of foolishness.
- **Back to the sources:** read the Bible and the ancient authors in their original words.
- **Peace:** real courage in a ruler is to curb greed, not to wage war.
- **Tolerance:** on matters that do not truly matter, Christians should live in concord.
What might surprise you

His moderation made him enemies on both sides. He pressed for reform of the Church, yet stayed in it and openly broke with Luther over free will. His middle road disappointed and angered partisans in both camps.

He is remembered with a link to Rotterdam, but he lived there only about four years and never went back. Today his name lives on in the EU's Erasmus programme, which sends students to study abroad.
Where to start reading
*The Praise of Folly* (1511): short, funny, and still sharp. Free on Project Gutenberg in White Kennett's old English translation.
sources: The app's Erasmus thoughts (#290–291), from *The Praise of Folly*

pages.title: Francis Bacon
sections: Who he was

Bacon was born in London in 1561, the son of one of Queen Elizabeth I's senior officials. He studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he came to find the Aristotle he was taught barren and argumentative. His father died before providing for him, and he spent years in debt.

He trained as a lawyer and rose slowly, then quickly under King James I. He became Attorney General in 1613 and later Lord Chancellor, the highest legal office in England, with the titles Baron Verulam and Viscount St Alban.

In 1621 he was found guilty of corruption. He was fined, held briefly in the Tower of London, and barred from public office. He spent his last years writing and died of pneumonia in 1626.
What he cared about

Bacon wanted knowledge that came from careful observation, not from old authorities. In his *Essays* he brought the same sharp eye to everyday life. His themes:

- **Learn from nature:** test ideas against what we actually observe, step by step.
- **Beware the mind's traps:** he called our habits of self-deception "idols of the mind".
- **Envy:** it always comes from comparing ourselves with others, especially those close to us.
- **Reading, talking, writing:** each shapes the mind differently, and we need all three.
- **Read with judgement:** some books are to be tasted, some swallowed, and a few chewed and digested.
What might surprise you

The father of empiricism may have died of an experiment. John Aubrey, who had the story from Thomas Hobbes, says Bacon stopped in the snow to test whether cold could preserve meat as salt does, stuffed a hen with snow, and fell fatally ill. The two events may be only a coincidence.

His public career had dark sides. As Attorney General, he used torture to win a treason conviction. Tried for bribery, he admitted taking gifts from people with cases before him, then a common custom, but insisted they never swayed his judgement.
Where to start reading
The *Essays* (final edition, 1625): 58 short pieces, a few pages each. "Of Studies" and "Of Envy" are good first choices. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Bacon thoughts (#609–610), from the *Essays* (1625)

pages.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who he was

Nietzsche grew up in Röcken, near Leipzig, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died when Friedrich was four. He was a brilliant student, and in 1869, at only 24, he became professor of classical philology at the University of Basel. He served briefly as a medical orderly in the Franco-Prussian War.

Ill for much of his life, he resigned in 1879 and lived as an independent writer, moving between Swiss mountain summers and Italian and French winters, often alone and short of money. In January 1889, in Turin, he suffered a mental breakdown from which he never recovered. He spent his last eleven years in the care of his mother and his sister.
What he cared about

Nietzsche wrote in aphorisms and poetic books like *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*. His big themes:

- **"God is dead":** with religion weakening, we must find new values and affirm life.
- **Become who you are:** create your own path instead of following the crowd.
- **Live dangerously:** growth comes from challenge, not comfort.
- **A friend should also be your best enemy,** pushing you to be better.
- **Eternal return:** could you love your life enough to live it again, forever?
What might surprise you

His sister, Elisabeth, took control of his writings and edited them to fit her own nationalist views. Through her editions, his name became linked with fascism and the Nazis, though he had openly opposed antisemitism and nationalism. Later scholars restored his texts.

He never married. He proposed three times to the writer Lou Salomé, and was turned down each time.
Where to start reading
*The Joyful Wisdom* (also called *The Gay Science*), Book IV: short sections, among his warmest writing. Thomas Common's translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Nietzsche thoughts (#209–216, #245, #256–260), from *Zarathustra*, *The Joyful Wisdom*, *Beyond Good and Evil*, and *Human, All-Too-Human*

pages.title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who he was

Dostoevsky was born in Moscow, trained as an engineer, and made his name with his first novel, *Poor Folk*, in the 1840s. In 1849 he was arrested for belonging to a circle that discussed banned books critical of the Tsar. He was sentenced to death, and the sentence was changed at the very last moment.

He then spent four years in a Siberian prison camp and six more as a soldier in exile. Back in St Petersburg, he wrote the novels that made him one of the greatest writers in any language: *Crime and Punishment*, *The Idiot*, *Demons*, and *The Brothers Karamazov*.
What he cared about

Dostoevsky wrote novels, but they are full of ideas, argued by characters who live them. His main questions:

- **Freedom:** people want to choose for themselves, even against their own interest.
- **Suffering:** what it does to us, and whether it can have meaning.
- **Faith and doubt:** he was a Russian Orthodox Christian, and his novels put that faith through hard tests.
- **Responsibility:** each of us is, in some way, responsible for everyone.
What might surprise you

The moment he faced the firing squad stayed with him for life, and he wrote it into *The Idiot*. Later, while travelling in Western Europe, he became addicted to gambling and at times had to beg for money.

His writings also contain negative stereotypes of Jews and other groups, and he denied being an enemy of the Jews when a reader accused him of it. Nietzsche called him the only psychologist he had learned anything from.
Where to start reading
*Notes from Underground* (1864): short, bitter, and darkly funny, and one of the first works of existentialist literature. Constance Garnett's translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Dostoevsky thoughts (#217–224, #246–249), from *Notes from Underground* and *The Brothers Karamazov*

pages.title: George Eliot
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who she was

George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, born in 1819 in Warwickshire, the daughter of an estate manager. She was a voracious reader with a religious schooling. In her twenties, friends introduced her to writers who questioned the literal truth of the Bible. As she began to doubt, her father threatened to throw her out, and she kept house for him until his death.

Her first big work was a translation of a German book on the life of Jesus. In 1850 she moved to London, where she wrote and edited for the radical *Westminster Review*. She also translated Spinoza's *Ethics*.

From 1854 she lived openly with the writer George Henry Lewes, who was married to someone else. She began writing fiction at 37, and her novels made her one of the great writers of her age. She died in 1880, months after marrying her younger friend John Cross.
What she cared about

Her novels look at ordinary people with deep attention and honesty. *Middlemarch* (1871–1872) is the best known. Her themes:

- **Sympathy:** we live to make life less difficult for each other.
- **The weight of ordinary pain:** if we truly felt all the suffering around us, we could not bear it.
- **Unhistoric acts:** much of the good in the world comes from quiet lives no one records.
- **Duty and work:** a good life is built from steady effort, not grand gestures.
- **Realism:** fiction should show people as they are, not as fantasies.
What might surprise you

She chose a man's name partly to protect her private life. Living with a married man was a scandal, and many people cut her off. When she died, her lack of Christian faith and her life with Lewes kept her out of Westminster Abbey.

She was also a sharp critic of other women writers. Her essay "Silly Novels by Lady Novelists" (1856) mocked the empty plots of popular fiction. Virginia Woolf later called *Middlemarch* "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people".
Where to start reading
*Middlemarch*: long, but it rewards every page. Start with the Prelude and the first book. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's George Eliot thoughts (#287–289), from *Middlemarch* (1871–1872)

pages.title: Hafiz
sections: Who he was

Hafiz was born in Shiraz, in what is now Iran, and spent nearly all his life there. We know few facts about him: even his birth year is uncertain, and most stories about his youth are later legends.

As a young man he learned the Quran by heart. "Hafiz", the title for someone who has done so, became his pen name. He was a Sufi, and he lived on the patronage of a series of rulers in Shiraz, some tolerant and some strict. Around 1368 he fell out of favour at court and only regained his place some 20 years later.

His fame spread in his lifetime. He exchanged letters and poems with the Sultan of Bengal. His poems were gathered into the *Divan*, probably after his death in 1390.
What he cared about

He wrote ghazals: short lyrics of love, wine, and longing that can be read as earthly love, love of God, or both. His themes:

- **Love is a hard road:** it looks easy from outside and asks a great deal from within.
- **Life is short:** our days are few, so meet them fully, like a rose that blooms without complaint.
- **Power passes:** the might of rulers lasts an hour, then nothing of it remains.
- **Against hypocrisy:** he exposes it wherever he finds it.
- **Mystery:** some gates stay locked to human wisdom, and he accepts that.
What might surprise you

In Iran, Hafiz is not only read but used. Many families keep his *Divan* at home. At Nowruz or on Yalda Night they open it at random and read the poem as a sign of what is coming. Many people know his lines by heart and quote them as everyday sayings.

His reach went far west too. Goethe's *West-Eastern Divan* (1819) was inspired by reading him in German translation, and Emerson called him "a poet's poet". His tomb in Shiraz is still a place people visit regularly.
Where to start reading
Gertrude Bell's *Poems from the Divan of Hafiz* (1897): a small selection in graceful English by the explorer and scholar. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Hafiz thoughts (#567–572, #598–599), from the *Divan*, translated by Gertrude Bell (1897)

pages.title: Henry David Thoreau
sections: Who he was

Thoreau was born in Concord, Massachusetts, the son of a pencil maker, and studied at Harvard. Back home, he became part of the circle around Ralph Waldo Emerson, the leading Transcendentalist. He earned his living in many small ways, including as a land surveyor, and filled his notebooks with close observations of nature.

In 1845 he built a small cabin on land Emerson owned, by Walden Pond, and lived there for two years and two months. He died of tuberculosis in 1862, aged 44.
What he cared about

*Walden* (1854) turns those years in the woods into one year, season by season. Its central ideas:

- **Live deliberately:** face only the essential facts of life, and see what they teach.
- **Simplify, simplify:** our lives are frittered away by detail.
- **Quiet desperation:** most people, he thought, are stuck in lives they never chose.
- **Your own drummer:** if you keep a different pace, perhaps you hear different music.
- **Resist injustice:** a citizen may refuse to obey an unjust state.
What might surprise you

In 1846 he refused to pay a tax, in protest against slavery and the war with Mexico, and spent a night in jail. Someone, probably his aunt, paid it against his wishes. The night led to his essay "Civil Disobedience", which later inspired Tolstoy, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.

He was also an active abolitionist and helped people escaping slavery on the Underground Railroad. And his life at Walden was less cut off than the book suggests: he sometimes took his laundry home to Concord to be washed.
Where to start reading
*Walden*, the chapter "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For". Free on Project Gutenberg.

pages.title: Heraclitus
sections: Who he was

Heraclitus lived around 500 BCE in Ephesus, a Greek city on the coast of today's Turkey, then part of the Persian Empire. We know very little about him. Most ancient stories about his life were probably invented later from his own sayings.

One story says he gave up the hereditary title of "king" to his younger brother, which at least suggests he came from a leading family. He seems to have had little sympathy for democracy or for the crowd.

He wrote a single book, later known as *On Nature*, and is said to have placed it in the great temple of Artemis. The book is lost. What survives is just over a hundred short fragments quoted by other writers.
What he cared about

Heraclitus saw a world in constant change, held together by a hidden order he called the *logos*. His themes:

- **Everything flows:** you cannot step into the same river twice, because the water is always new.
- **Opposites belong together:** the way up and the way down are one and the same.
- **Harmony in strife:** conflict and tension are part of how the world holds together.
- **Learning is not understanding:** knowing many facts does not make you wise.
- **Look inward:** "I inquired of myself", and a person's character is their guardian spirit.
What might surprise you

Even the ancients found him hard. His riddling style earned him the names "the dark" and "the obscure". He was seen as proud and gloomy, and later art paired him as "the weeping philosopher" with Democritus, "the laughing philosopher".

He was also scornful. He mocked Homer, Hesiod, and Pythagoras, along with the religious rites of his day. Yet his few lines shaped Plato, the Stoics, Hegel, Nietzsche, and Heidegger.
Where to start reading
The fragments themselves: a few pages that take a lifetime. Arthur Fairbanks's translation in *The First Philosophers of Greece* (1898) is free online.
sources: The app's Heraclitus thoughts (#121–125, #132–134), from the *Fragments*, translated by Arthur Fairbanks (1898)

pages.title: Ibn Arabi
sections: Who he was

Ibn Arabi was born in 1165 in Murcia, in Muslim Spain, and grew up in Seville, where his family served the ruler. As a boy he preferred military games to books. Then, as a teenager, he had a vision that turned him towards the Sufi path.

His father mentioned the change to the great philosopher Averroes, who asked to meet him. Ibn Arabi said the meeting taught him the difference between knowledge gained by reasoning and insight that comes by unveiling.

At 33 he left Spain for good. He travelled for 25 years, through North Africa, Mecca, Baghdad, and Anatolia, then settled in Damascus in 1223 to teach and write. He died there in 1240.
What he cared about

Ibn Arabi was a mystic, philosopher, and poet who wrote in Arabic, not Persian: he belongs to this path as a Sufi master whose ideas spread across the Islamic world. About 800 works are attributed to him. His themes:

- **The unity of being:** everything that exists is a face of one single reality, God.
- **A heart open to every form:** a true lover can find the divine in a monastery, a temple, or the Kaaba.
- **Love as a religion:** he follows love wherever it leads.
- **Imagination:** not a trick of the mind but a real way of knowing the world.
- **The complete human:** a person who joins the divine and the created world in themselves.
What might surprise you

His love poems are also theology. *The Interpreter of Desires* reads like a collection of classic Arabic love odes, yet he wrote a commentary explaining them as mystical poems. The famous lines on a heart that can hold every form come from it.

He was, and still is, contested. Many jurists saw him as a heretic, while Sufis called him "the Greatest Master" and some Muslims revere him as a saint. His ideas spread quickly across the Islamic world after his death.
Where to start reading
*The Interpreter of Desires* (*Tarjumán al-Ashwáq*): short odes with his own notes. R. A. Nicholson's 1911 translation is free on Wikisource.
sources: The app's Ibn Arabi thoughts (#577), from *The Tarjumán al-Ashwáq*, translated by R. A. Nicholson (1911)

pages.title: Immanuel Kant
sections: Who he was

Kant was born in Königsberg, in Prussia, the fourth of nine children in a strict and devout Pietist family. After his father's death interrupted his studies, he worked for some years as a private tutor in towns around Königsberg, then returned to lecture at its university, where he became a professor in 1770.

He was a popular teacher and a sociable man, but he lived by a strict routine: it was said that neighbours set their watches by his daily walk. He twice thought of marrying, waited too long both times, and stayed single. His *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781) made him one of the central thinkers of the Enlightenment.
What he cared about

Kant wanted to show what we can know, and what we must do. On ethics, his key ideas:

- **The only thing good without condition** is a good will.
- **Treat people as ends,** never only as means, yourself included.
- **Morality is not about being happy,** but about becoming worthy of happiness.
- **Duty from reason:** the moral law binds every rational being, whatever their wishes.
- **Awe:** the starry sky above us and the moral law within us.
What might surprise you

The philosopher of human dignity also wrote openly racist things, and denied women full capacity for moral reasoning. Few scholars dispute this; they debate how much it undermines the rest of his work.

He also thought hard about peace. In *Towards Perpetual Peace* (1795) he argued that treaties alone cannot end wars: lasting peace needs republican constitutions, international law, and a free federation of states.
Where to start reading
*Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals*, First Section: short, and the clearest way into his ethics. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott's translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Kant thoughts (#152–157, #206–208), from the *Groundwork* and the *Critique of Practical Reason*

pages.title: Jean de La Bruyère
sections: Who he was

La Bruyère was born in Paris in 1645 to a middle-class family. He trained as a lawyer and in 1673 bought a post in the tax office at Caen, which gave him an income and some standing.

Through the churchman Bossuet he found a place in 1684 in the household of the Prince of Condé, one of the greatest nobles in France. He became tutor to the prince's grandson and spent the rest of his life there, watching the powerful up close.

What he saw went into *The Characters* (1688). He was elected to the Académie française in 1693, after three defeats, and died suddenly in 1696.
What he cared about

*The Characters* is a book of short remarks and sharp portraits of the people of his time. His themes:

- **Forgetting to live:** we do not feel our birth, we suffer our death, and we forget the living in between.
- **The present:** children enjoy the moment, something adults rarely manage.
- **Conversation:** the art lies less in showing your own wit than in helping others find theirs.
- **Knowing when to be quiet:** it is a misfortune to have neither the wit to speak well nor the judgement to stay silent.
- **Vanity and status:** the court's climbers, flatterers, and snobs, drawn without mercy.
What might surprise you

Readers loved guessing who was who. Copies of "keys" passed around Paris, naming the real people behind his portraits. He denied that any portrait showed a single person, but many recognised themselves and became his enemies, and they blocked his way into the Académie for years.

He mocked people who invented noble ancestors, and he signed his name as one word, Delabruyère, to show it. Yet those who met him describe a silent, watchful, rather awkward man, far from the sharp voice of his book.
Where to start reading
*The Characters*, the chapters "Of Man" and "Of Society and Conversation": short remarks you can read a few at a time. Free on Project Gutenberg; the app uses its own translations from the French.
sources: The app's La Bruyère thoughts (#626–629), from *The Characters*

pages.title: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
sections: Who he was

Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712, the son of a watchmaker. His mother died nine days after his birth. Apprenticed to an engraver who beat him, he left Geneva as a teenager and drifted through Savoy and France.

In Paris he became a friend of Diderot and wrote for the *Encyclopédie*. Fame came suddenly in 1750, when his essay arguing that the arts and sciences had corrupted naturally good people won a prize. He also wrote music, and his opera *The Village Soothsayer* pleased King Louis XV.

In 1762 he published *The Social Contract* and *Emile*. Both were condemned: his books were burned and warrants issued for his arrest. He spent years moving from refuge to refuge, grew fearful of plots against him, and died at Ermenonville in 1778.
What he cared about

Rousseau asked why people born good and free end up unequal and unhappy. His themes:

- **Freedom lost in society:** people are born free, yet everywhere live in chains of their own making.
- **Inequality:** private property, he argued, is where social inequality begins.
- **Citizens, not spectators:** a free people takes part in its shared affairs; once citizens stop caring, the state is lost.
- **Feeling, not just years:** the one who has lived most is the one who has most felt life.
- **Vanity:** much unhappiness comes from caring only about our standing against others.
What might surprise you

The great writer on education gave away his own children. By his own account, he and Thérèse Levasseur, later his wife, had five children, and all were left at a foundling hospital soon after birth, then almost a death sentence. Later in life he said he regretted it.

His picture of the family also rested on women serving men. In *Emile* he argued that girls should be educated to please men, which is why Mary Wollstonecraft attacked him by name. His later books, the *Confessions* and the *Reveries of the Solitary Walker*, turn inward, looking closely at his own feelings and memories.
Where to start reading
*The Social Contract*, Book I: short chapters, and the famous opening line. Free on Project Gutenberg in English; the app uses its own translations from the French.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Jean Jacques Rousseau"
Wikipedia, "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman"
The app's Rousseau thoughts (#617–622), from *The Social Contract*, *Emile*, the *Reveries*, and the *Discourse on Inequality*

pages.title: John Locke
sections: Who he was

Locke was born in 1632 to Puritan parents in Somerset, England. He grew up through the civil war, the execution of King Charles I, and the return of the monarchy. He studied at Oxford and stayed 15 years, drawn more to medicine and experiment than to the old curriculum.

In 1666 a chance meeting brought him into the household of Lord Shaftesbury, a leading politician. As his doctor, Locke oversaw a risky operation that Shaftesbury credited with saving his life. When Shaftesbury fell from favour, Locke fled to the Dutch Republic in 1683.

He came home after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and published his major works within a year or two. He spent his last 14 years in the country house of his friend, the philosopher Lady Masham, and died there in 1704.
What he cared about

Locke asked where our knowledge comes from and what makes a government legitimate. His themes:

- **The mind as a blank slate:** we are born without ready-made ideas; everything we know comes from experience.
- **Government by consent:** rulers hold power only with the people's consent, and a tyrant who loses it may be resisted.
- **Law protects freedom:** good law does not shrink our liberty; it preserves and enlarges it.
- **Toleration:** faith is a personal matter, and churches should not force belief.
- **New ideas deserve a hearing:** a truth is no less true for being new.
What might surprise you

The "father of liberalism" was tied to the slave trade. He held shares in a company that traded enslaved Africans, and he helped draft the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, which gave colonists absolute power over their slaves. Historians still debate how far he shared those views.

He also kept his name off his own revolution. *Two Treatises of Government* and *A Letter Concerning Toleration* came out anonymously. Their ideas later shaped the language of the American Declaration of Independence.
Where to start reading
*Second Treatise of Government*, chapters 2 to 9: the core of his case for freedom and consent. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Locke thoughts (#624–625), from *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* and the *Second Treatise of Government* (1690)

pages.title: John Stuart Mill
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who he was

Mill was born in London, the eldest son of the philosopher James Mill, who educated him at home with help from Jeremy Bentham. He learned Greek at three, and by eight had read the whole of the historian Herodotus. From the age of 17, he worked for 35 years for the East India Company, as his father had.

At twenty, the strain caught up with him: he went through months of deep sadness, and the poetry of Wordsworth helped him find joy again. In 1851 he married Harriet Taylor, his close friend of twenty years, whose ideas shaped his work. Later he served as a Member of Parliament, and he died in Avignon, where she is buried, in 1873.
What he cared about

Mill is often called the most influential English-speaking philosopher of the 19th century. His central themes:

- **Liberty:** you may pursue your own good in your own way, as long as you do not harm others.
- **Free speech:** silencing even one dissenting voice robs everyone, since we learn by hearing the other side.
- **Individuality:** human nature is not a machine but a tree, which needs room to grow.
- **Happiness,** but of a higher kind: better a dissatisfied human than a satisfied pig.
- **Women's equality,** argued in *The Subjection of Women* (1869).
What might surprise you

As an MP, he tried to change the Reform Bill to give the vote to every "person" instead of every "man". He was only the second member of Parliament to call for women's suffrage. He was also the godfather of the philosopher Bertrand Russell.

His defence of liberty had limits, though. In *On Liberty* he called despotism a legitimate way to govern people he called "barbarians", provided it improved them, a view tied to the empire he served for most of his career.
Where to start reading
*On Liberty* (1859), chapters I to III. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: John Stuart Mill, *On Liberty*, chapter I (Project Gutenberg)
The app's Mill thoughts (#158–167, #197–205), including #158, #160, #164, and #197

pages.title: Kamo no Chōmei
pages.era: Japan, from the Heian court to the age of the samurai
sections: Who he was

Chōmei was the second son of the head priest of the Lower Kamo Shinto shrine in Kyoto. He grew up at court, loved music, and was known as a fine player of the *biwa*, a Japanese lute. In his thirties his poems won contests and appeared in anthologies, and the retired emperor Go-Toba appointed him to his Imperial Poetry Office.

But he lost his political backing and was passed over for the post at his family's shrine; a cousin got it instead. In 1204 he turned his back on society, took Buddhist vows, and became a hermit. After a few years at the foot of Mount Hiei, he built a tiny hut in the hills of Hino, south-east of the capital, and lived there for the rest of his life.
What he cared about

In the hut he wrote *Hōjōki*, *An Account of a Ten-Foot-Square Hut* (1212). It opens with a river that never stops flowing and is never the same water. His themes:

- **Impermanence:** people and houses are like foam on the water, here and gone.
- **Disaster:** fires, a whirlwind, famine, and an earthquake that struck Kyoto in his lifetime.
- **Owning less:** a small, movable hut is enough, and frees you from worry.
- **Solitude:** music, poems, and walks in the hills as company.
What might surprise you

He was an unusual hermit for his time. Most people who left the world joined a monastery; Chōmei lived alone instead.

He is also more human than his serene book suggests. He still held a grudge against the cousin who took the shrine post. And though he writes in *Hōjōki* that he never left his hut, another account says he made at least one journey away from it.
Where to start reading
*Hōjōki*: only a few dozen pages. W. G. Aston's 1899 translation, in *A History of Japanese Literature*, is free online.

pages.title: Kenkō
pages.era: Japan, from the Heian court to the age of the samurai
sections: Who he was

Kenkō was the son of an official and served as an officer of the guards at the imperial palace in Kyoto. Later in life he left public life and became a Buddhist monk and hermit.

Nobody knows why. One story says it was an unhappy love; another, grief at the death of a former emperor. He kept writing poetry and took part in poetry contests at court, but his fame rests on one book, written between 1330 and 1332.
What he cared about

*Essays in Idleness* is a collection of 243 short pieces, from a single line to a few pages. He wrote in a "follow the brush" style, letting one thought lead to the next. His main themes:

- **Impermanence:** everything passes, and that is part of its beauty.
- **Death:** it comes sooner than we think, so do not waste your days.
- **Nature and small things:** flowers before they bloom, a garden strewn with fallen ones, the moon as it wanes.
- **People:** friendship, manners, and the follies of those around him.
What might surprise you

For a monk writing about death, Kenkō is often funny. He tells little stories from everyday life, like the archery teacher who tells a beginner to carry only one arrow, and he has firm views on taste: a little imperfection, he says, beats perfect sameness.

The book was not published in his lifetime and was not even divided into numbered passages until the 17th century. Even his name has a twist: "Yoshida Kenkō" comes from later documents that recent research has shown to be forged.
Where to start reading
*Essays in Idleness*: open it anywhere and read one passage at a time. William N. Porter's 1914 translation, *A Miscellany of a Japanese Priest*, is free on archive.org.
sources: The app's Kenkō thoughts (#515–527, #546–547) and their translations

pages.title: La Rochefoucauld
sections: Who he was

La Rochefoucauld was born in Paris into one of the greatest noble families of France. He was married at fourteen and commanding a regiment at sixteen. As a young courtier he plotted against the powerful Cardinal Richelieu, which earned him eight days in the Bastille and spells of exile from court.

In the 1640s and 1650s he joined the Fronde, a rebellion of nobles against the crown, and was badly wounded in the fighting. After that he withdrew from politics, wrote his memoirs, and became a regular of the Paris literary salons.
What he cared about

In 1665 he published, anonymously, his *Maxims*: in the end 504 short sayings, most just two or three lines. They look hard at why people really act:

- **Self-love:** much of what we call virtue is self-interest in disguise.
- **Disguise:** we hide from others for so long that in the end we hide from ourselves.
- **Love and friendship** are rarely as pure as we claim.
- **Hypocrisy:** even false virtue is a tribute, since hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.
What might surprise you

Many readers find the *Maxims* cynical, even bitter. Yet they grew out of a social game. In the salon of the Marquise de Sablé, guests polished short sayings together, and La Rochefoucauld kept revising his for the rest of his life.

He also tried to escape his own reputation: when a version of his memoirs appeared without his consent, he denied it was genuine, but few people believed him.
Where to start reading
The *Maxims*: open them anywhere and read three or four at a time. The 1871 translation by J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's La Rochefoucauld thoughts (#271–275, #286, #299–302), from the *Maxims*

pages.title: Laozi
sections: Who he was

We are not sure. The earliest accounts say Laozi, "the Old Master", was a man called Li Er or Lao Dan, who kept the archives at the Zhou court and was an older contemporary of Confucius. Scholars are divided: some accept that a Lao Dan probably lived, others see him as largely or wholly a legend.

The best-known story says that, at the age of 80, he set off west to live as a hermit. At the last gate, a guard named Yinxi recognised him and asked him to write down his wisdom before leaving. What he wrote, the story goes, was the *Tao Te Ching*.
What he cared about

- **The Tao:** the way of all things, which cannot be fully named.
- **Effortless action:** the wise act without forcing, and things get done.
- **Water as a model:** soft and low, it serves everything and wears down the hardest stone.
- **Less is more:** fewer desires, fewer possessions, fewer rules.
- **Quiet leadership:** the best rulers are barely noticed.
What might surprise you

The oldest pieces of the *Tao Te Ching* ever found were written on bamboo strips buried around 300 BCE. They hold only about 40 percent of the text we read today, which suggests the book grew over time.

Later, Laozi became far more than a writer. From the Han dynasty on, religious Taoism worshipped him as a god, and the Tang emperors claimed him as their ancestor.
Where to start reading
The *Tao Te Ching*: 81 short chapters, best read one at a time. James Legge's 1891 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Laozi thoughts (#410–428, #441–451), including #410, #422, and #442

pages.title: Leo Tolstoy
pages.era: Europe and Russia in the 19th century
sections: Who he was

Tolstoy was born in 1828 into a family of Russian counts, on the estate of Yasnaya Polyana south of Moscow. His mother died when he was two and his father when he was nine. He left university without a degree, ran up gambling debts, and joined the army, serving as an artillery officer in the siege of Sevastopol.

In 1862 he married Sophia Behrs, and they had 13 children, eight of whom survived childhood. In the years that followed he wrote *War and Peace* (1869) and *Anna Karenina* (1878), often named among the greatest novels ever written.

Then, in his early fifties, came a crisis of meaning, and a turn to a radical, personal Christianity. He gave up meat and tried to give up his wealth. In 1910, aged 82, he set off on a train journey and died of pneumonia at a small railway station.
What he cared about

*A Confession* (written 1879–1880) tells how success stopped meaning anything to him, and how he searched for a reason to live. His themes:

- **The question of meaning:** if death is certain, what is the point of what I do today?
- **Success is not an answer:** fame, family, and wealth did not save him from despair.
- **Honesty about despair:** he describes the crisis plainly, without dressing it up.
- **Faith as a way of living:** he came to read the Sermon on the Mount literally, as rules for life.
- **Non-violence:** never resist evil by force, a view that later shaped Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
What might surprise you

The author of *War and Peace* came to reject his own great novels, along with most of modern Western culture. His ideas also led the Russian Orthodox Church to excommunicate him in 1901, and the Church's censors cut *A Confession* from the journal that first tried to print it.

His home life suffered as his views hardened. His wish to give away his wealth and the copyrights to his books caused deep conflict with his wife. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize several times and never won it.
Where to start reading
*A Confession*: short, direct, and personal. Aylmer Maude's English translation is free on Standard Ebooks.
sources: The app's Tolstoy thoughts (#243–244), from *A Confession*, translated by Aylmer Maude

pages.title: Lucretius
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: Who he was

We know almost nothing about Lucretius's life. The only sure fact is that he was a friend, or a client, of a Roman politician named Gaius Memmius, to whom he dedicated his one surviving work. He lived in the last, violent years of the Roman Republic, in the age of Cicero.

That work is *On the Nature of Things*, a long poem in Latin that sets out the philosophy of Epicurus. It shaped the great Roman poets who came after him, above all Virgil.
What he cared about

Lucretius used poetry to carry Epicurus's ideas to Roman readers. His aim was to free them from fear:

- **Nothing comes from nothing,** and nothing ever returns to nothing.
- **The world is made of tiny particles** moving in empty space, always coming together and falling apart.
- **Fear comes from ignorance:** people blame the gods for what they do not understand.
- **Death is no evil:** leave life like a guest who has eaten well at a banquet.
- **Everything changes:** nations rise and fall, and drops of water wear away stone.
What might surprise you

The poem was almost lost. It survived the Middle Ages in very few copies until an Italian book hunter, Poggio Bracciolini, found one in a German monastery in 1417. It then fed the revival of atomism in early modern science, and Montaigne owned and annotated a copy.

A strange legend, recorded by Saint Jerome four centuries later, says Lucretius was driven mad by a love potion and took his own life. Scholars doubt it, not least because the same ancient notes get other basic facts about him wrong.
Where to start reading
*On the Nature of Things*, Book I, especially the opening sections on atoms and fear. William Ellery Leonard's 1916 verse translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Lucretius thoughts (#74–76, #87–94), from *On the Nature of Things*

pages.title: Marcus Aurelius
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: Who he was

Marcus lost his father at three and was raised by his mother and grandfather. In 138, the emperor Hadrian chose Antoninus Pius as his heir, and Antoninus in turn adopted Marcus. As heir to the throne, Marcus studied Greek and Latin with the best teachers of his time.

He became emperor in 161 and ruled until his death in 180. It was a hard reign: wars in the East and along the Danube, and a plague that killed millions across the empire. He is remembered as the last of the "Five Good Emperors".
What he cared about

The *Meditations* are his private notes, written in Greek, many of them in army camps. He probably never meant them to be published. He keeps coming back to a few ideas:

- **Do your duty** today, well, without waiting for thanks.
- **We are made to work together,** like the hands and feet of one body.
- **Your mind is yours:** things cannot disturb you, only your judgments about them.
- **Everything passes,** including fame, so do not chase it.
What might surprise you

The most powerful man in the world filled his notes with reminders to be patient and humble. Yet his reign was far from peaceful, and he spent years at war.

Persecution of Christians appears to have grown in his time, though historians think he was unlikely to have ordered it. He was also succeeded by his son, Commodus, and historians still debate that choice.
Where to start reading
*Meditations*, Book II: short and direct, and it opens with his famous advice for the start of each day. George Long's 1862 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Marcus Aurelius thoughts (#1–14, #32–39), including #32 (Meditations 2.1)

pages.title: Margaret Fuller
sections: Who she was

Fuller was born in Cambridgeport, Massachusetts. Her father, a lawyer, gave her an education as demanding as any boy's: she was translating Virgil from Latin as a small child. By her thirties she was known as the best-read person in New England, and she was the first woman allowed to use Harvard's library.

From 1839 she ran "Conversations", discussion classes for women who had no access to higher education. Emerson made her the first editor of the Transcendentalist journal *The Dial*. In 1844 she joined the *New-York Tribune* as a critic, the first full-time book reviewer in American journalism.
What she cared about

Her book *Woman in the Nineteenth Century* (1845) is considered the first major feminist work in the United States. Its key points:

- **Every path should be open to women** as freely as to men.
- **Self-reliance is for everyone:** independence praised in men is called a fault in women.
- **Growth:** people, women and men, are made to expand, not to be held in narrow roles.
- **Education:** women deserve the same chance to learn and think as men.
What might surprise you

In 1846 the *Tribune* sent her to Europe as its first female foreign correspondent. In Italy she joined the side of the 1848 revolutions. During the siege of Rome she volunteered in hospitals, while her partner, Giovanni Ossoli, fought on the walls.

In 1850 she sailed home with Ossoli and their child. The ship sank off Fire Island, near New York, and all three died; her body was never found. The leaders of the women's suffrage movement later wrote that she had more influence on American women's thinking than any woman before her.
Where to start reading
*Woman in the Nineteenth Century*: bold and still fresh. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Fuller thoughts (#293–295), from *Woman in the Nineteenth Century*

pages.title: Mary Wollstonecraft
tags: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
sections: Who she was

Mary Wollstonecraft was born in 1759 in Spitalfields, London. Her father was a violent man who beat her mother in drunken rages. As a teenager, Mary would lie outside her mother's bedroom door to protect her.

She had few options as a poor but respectable woman. She ran a school at Newington Green with her sisters and her friend Fanny Blood, then worked as a governess in Ireland. Back in London, the publisher Joseph Johnson gave her work as a translator and reviewer, and she began to live by her pen.

Her reply to Edmund Burke, *A Vindication of the Rights of Men* (1790), made her famous overnight. Two years later came *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*. She went to revolutionary Paris, had a daughter with the American Gilbert Imlay, and tried to take her own life after he left her.

She then married the philosopher William Godwin. She died in 1797, aged 38, eleven days after giving birth to Mary Shelley, the future author of *Frankenstein*.
What she cared about

She believed women seemed weaker than men only because they were denied a real education. Her themes:

- **Reason has no sex:** men and women are both rational beings and should be treated as such.
- **Education for all:** girls and boys taught together, in the same way.
- **Partners, not ornaments:** a wife should be her husband's companion, not property traded in marriage.
- **Independence:** a woman who depends on others for her body and her bread will soon depend on them for her thoughts.
- **Liberty makes people better:** freer societies make people wiser and more virtuous, women included.
What might surprise you

Her most famous book was written to change one man's mind. In 1791 the French statesman Talleyrand proposed that girls receive only a domestic education. She also attacked Rousseau, who argued in *Emile* that women should be educated to please men.

She was not a modern feminist in every way. It is unclear whether she wanted women to vote, she wrote mainly for the middle class, and she could be harsh about the women of her day, calling the frivolous ones spaniels and toys.

After her death, Godwin published a frank memoir of her unconventional life. It wrecked her reputation for almost a century, until the feminist movement rediscovered her.
Where to start reading
*A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*: long and passionate, but the opening chapters set out all its main topics. Free on Project Gutenberg; the app quotes her original English.
sources: Wikipedia, "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman"
The app's Wollstonecraft thoughts (#178–179, #192–193), from *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*

pages.title: Mencius
sections: Who he was

Mencius, born Meng Ke, came from the small state of Zou, in eastern China, about a century after Confucius. He lost his father young, and his mother, who raised him, became a model of wise parenting in Chinese tradition. He is said to have studied in the school of Confucius's grandson, Zisi.

Like Confucius, he spent years travelling from court to court, advising rulers during the violent Warring States period. He served for a time as an official and scholar in the state of Qi, and left to mourn his mother for three years. Disappointed that rulers ignored his advice, he finally withdrew from public life.
What he cared about

The book named after him, the *Mencius*, records his conversations with rulers and students. His central claim: human nature is good.

- **Anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well** feels alarm at once, without thinking of reward. That is the seed of goodness in all of us.
- **Four beginnings:** compassion, shame, respect, and a sense of right and wrong, which we must grow like plants.
- **Shame matters:** a person without it cannot become good.
- **Rulers serve the people:** a state that governs humanely will flourish.
What might surprise you

The gentle optimist was also a political radical for his time. He argued that people may overthrow, or even kill, a ruler who ignores their needs and rules harshly, because such a ruler is no longer a true ruler.

His view of human nature set him against another Confucian, Xunzi, who thought people are born bad. Centuries later, his book became one of the Four Books at the core of Confucian education, and he is honoured as the "Second Sage".
Where to start reading
The *Mencius*, Book II, Part I, with the child at the well. James Legge's 1895 translation is free online.

pages.title: Michel de Montaigne
sections: Who he was

Montaigne grew up on his family's estate near Bordeaux, in a wealthy family whose fortune began with a herring merchant. His father had an unusual plan for him: Latin was to be his first language, taught by a German tutor who spoke no French.

He trained in law and worked as a magistrate in Bordeaux, where he met his great friend Étienne de La Boétie. In 1571, on his 38th birthday, he withdrew to a tower of his château, with a library of some 1,500 books. There he began the *Essays*, first published in 1580, and kept adding to them until his death.
What he cared about

Montaigne's subject was himself, as an example of being human. His big themes:

- **What do I know?** His famous question: doubt, especially about our own certainties.
- **Learning to die** is learning to be free.
- **Living well** is about how we use our time, not how long we live.
- **Other cultures:** we call barbarous whatever is not our own custom.
- **Honesty:** to be the same inside as outside.
What might surprise you

He wrote in the middle of France's brutal wars between Catholics and Protestants. A Catholic himself, he was trusted by both sides, and acted as a moderating voice between the Catholic king and the Protestant Henry of Navarre.

From 1578 he suffered from painful kidney stones, and still avoided doctors and drugs. His *Essays*, translated into English in 1603, very likely influenced Shakespeare: a scene in *The Tempest* closely follows one of them.
Where to start reading
"That to Study Philosophy Is to Learn to Die" or "Of Cannibals", two short essays from Book I. Charles Cotton's translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Montaigne thoughts (#276–285, #303–304), including #277, #278, #281, and #304

pages.title: Niccolò Machiavelli
sections: Who he was

Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469. From 1498 to 1512, while the Medici family was out of power, he served the Florentine Republic as a senior official in charge of diplomatic and military affairs. His missions let him watch rulers like Cesare Borgia build states up close.

He also raised a citizen militia, which took Pisa in 1509. But in 1512 the Medici returned and he lost his post. Wrongly suspected of plotting against them, he was jailed and tortured, then freed under an amnesty three weeks later.

He retired to his farm outside Florence and became a writer. There, around 1513, he wrote *The Prince*. It was published in 1532, five years after his death.
What he cared about

Machiavelli wanted to describe politics as it is, not as it should be. His themes:

- **Feared or loved:** if a ruler cannot be both, fear is safer, but he must never be hated.
- **Appearances:** most people judge by what they see; few know who you really are.
- **Act early:** problems are easy to cure but hard to see at first, and easy to see but hard to cure later.
- **Change is hard:** whoever brings a new order makes enemies of all who gained from the old one.
- **Virtù and fortune:** a ruler's skill and daring matter, and so does fortune, which he must always reckon with.
What might surprise you

The man behind "Machiavellian" was a lifelong republican. His *Discourses on Livy* (around 1517) has been called a founding text of modern republicanism. Some 18th-century readers, Rousseau among them, even read *The Prince* as satire, though most scholars disagree.

Still, the book's hard edges are real. He admired Cesare Borgia and held that fraud, deceit, and violence can be necessary to keep power. In 1559 the Catholic Church put *The Prince* on its list of banned books.
Where to start reading
*The Prince*, chapters 15 to 18: the famous pages on how rulers should behave. W. K. Marriott's translation (1908) is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Machiavelli thoughts (#605–608), from *The Prince*, translated by W. K. Marriott (1908)

pages.title: Nicolas Chamfort
sections: Who he was

Chamfort was born around 1741 in Clermont-Ferrand; sources differ on the date and raised by a grocer. Local tradition said he was the secret child of a noblewoman and a clergyman. At nine he went to Paris on a scholarship, and later lived for years on the hospitality of people who enjoyed his conversation.

Success came slowly, then all at once. His plays were performed before Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, he received royal pensions, and in 1781 he was elected to the Académie française. But he disliked court life and kept stepping away from it.

When the Revolution came, he threw himself into it. He was among the first to enter the Bastille and served as secretary of the Jacobin club. Then his jokes turned on the new rulers, and during the Terror he was jailed. Threatened with arrest again, he tried to take his own life, and he died of his wounds months later, in April 1794.
What he cared about

Chamfort left notes of maxims and anecdotes, published after his death as *Maxims and Thoughts*. His themes:

- **Laughter:** the most wasted day is the one without it.
- **Society's masks:** he watched the salons and the court closely and showed what lay behind the manners.
- **Freedom:** he hated servility, whether to a king or to a revolution.
- **Self-made knowledge:** he joked that he had forgotten what he was taught and only knew what he had guessed.
- **Books over people:** the great dead, he said, make better company than the living.
What might surprise you

His wit cost him his life. A republican through and through, he could not stop mocking the revolutionary government, and it was his sarcasm, not royalism, that made him a suspect.

His maxims are often set beside La Rochefoucauld's. They are less polished but more violent, written in a time of storm. John Stuart Mill praised them highly.
Where to start reading
*Maxims and Thoughts*: short and sharp, best read a few at a time. Free in French on Project Gutenberg; the app uses its own translations.
sources: The app's Chamfort thoughts (#630), from *Maxims and Thoughts*

pages.title: Okakura Kakuzō
sections: Who he was

Okakura grew up in Yokohama, studying Western culture at school and Japanese tradition in a Buddhist temple. At the Tokyo Imperial University he studied with the American art historian Ernest Fenollosa, and he went on to work for the Ministry of Education.

In 1887 he helped found the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, and he soon became its director. When it began to favour European methods, he resigned and started a new academy with leading artists, to learn from Western art without losing Japanese inspiration. From 1906 he worked at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, where he became curator of Japanese and Chinese art.
What he cared about

He wrote his main works in English, to speak directly to Western readers. In *The Book of Tea* (1906), tea becomes a way of seeing life:

- **The beauty of the imperfect:** true beauty is found by one who completes the incomplete in the mind.
- **Emptiness is useful:** a pitcher's value lies in the space where water goes.
- **Leave something unsaid,** so others can finish the thought.
- **Small things reveal us:** the art of life lies in everyday details.
- **East and West can complete each other,** if each learns to respect the other.
What might surprise you

*The Book of Tea* was partly a reply. Written just after the Russo-Japanese War, it protested Western caricatures of Japan, and the fear that Japan was respected only once it adopted the West's taste for war.

He also spent two years in India and talked with Vivekananda and Tagore, two other voices in the app. In Boston, he once hosted a tea ceremony by candlelight for the art collector Isabella Stewart Gardner.
Where to start reading
*The Book of Tea*, chapter I. Short, warm, and written in English. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Okakura thoughts (#528–537, #550–554), from *The Book of Tea*

pages.title: Omar Khayyam
sections: Who he was

Omar Khayyam was born in Nishapur, in north-east Persia, and lived under the Seljuk sultans, around the time of the First Crusade. He was first of all a scientist. In mathematics, he found a general way to solve cubic equations using geometry, centuries before Descartes.

In 1074 the sultan Malik-Shah called him to his service and asked him to set up an observatory in Isfahan. There Khayyam measured the length of the solar year with great precision and designed a new calendar, which is still the basis of the Persian calendar today.
What he cared about

The short four-line poems, or quatrains, attributed to him are full of questions, doubt, and a love of the present:

- **Time cannot be undone:** the moving finger writes, and nothing will cancel a line.
- **We cannot see behind the veil:** the great questions stay without answers.
- **Learned arguments go round in circles,** and we come out by the same door we went in.
- **Enjoy the present:** a book of verses, bread, wine, and good company.
- **Everything passes,** sultans and their glory included.
What might surprise you

We are not sure he wrote the poems at all. No collection survives from his lifetime, and some scholars think the whole tradition of "Khayyam's quatrains" may have been attached to his name later.

In his own time, his doubts made religious leaders suspicious, and after he fell from favour at court he made the pilgrimage to Mecca, perhaps partly to prove his faith. In the West he became famous through Edward FitzGerald's free English version of 1859, which the Pre-Raphaelites came to admire.
Where to start reading
FitzGerald's *Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám*, first edition (1859): 75 quatrains, read in ten minutes, and free on Project Gutenberg. Remember it is FitzGerald's poem as much as Khayyam's.
sources: The app's Omar Khayyam thoughts (#579–586), from FitzGerald's *Rubáiyát*

pages.title: Petrarch
sections: Who he was

Francesco Petrarca was born in Arezzo, in Tuscany, in 1304, and grew up mostly near Avignon, where the popes then lived. His father, a notary, made him study law, but he cared far more for Latin literature.

In 1327, in a church in Avignon, he saw a woman he called Laura. She became the subject of his love poems for the rest of his life, even after her death in 1348. His Latin epic *Africa* made him famous, and in 1341 he was crowned poet laureate in Rome.

He worked for the Church, travelled widely as a scholar and diplomat, and collected crumbling old Latin manuscripts. He spent his last years in the village of Arquà, near Padua, and died there in 1374.
What he cared about

Petrarch wanted to bring the wisdom of ancient Rome back to life and use it to live better. His themes:

- **The classics:** his rediscovery of Cicero's letters helped start the Renaissance.
- **Knowing yourself:** in his *Secret* he argues with Saint Augustine about his own failings.
- **The struggle with our faults:** the pain of seeing them clearly and still not breaking free.
- **Love and longing:** his sonnets to Laura became a model for poets across Europe.
- **Curiosity:** he travelled for the pleasure of seeing, not only for duty.
What might surprise you

He has been called "the first tourist". In 1336 he climbed Mont Ventoux in Provence just for the view, then opened Augustine's *Confessions* at the top and read it as a lesson about his own soul.

He also invented the idea of the "Dark Ages" for the centuries after Rome, a label most historians now find misleading. And though his Church career meant he could not marry, he had two children, a son and a daughter, whom he later recognised.
Where to start reading
*Petrarch's Secret*: an imagined dialogue with Augustine, honest and searching. William H. Draper's 1911 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Petrarch thoughts (#292), from *Petrarch's Secret*, translated by William H. Draper (1911)

pages.title: Plato
sections: Who he was

Plato was born into an old, influential Athenian family. As a young man he hoped for a life in politics. But in 404 BCE, after Athens lost its long war with Sparta, a brutal regime known as the Thirty Tyrants took power, and two of his own relatives were among them. He refused to join them.

Five years later, the restored democracy put his teacher Socrates on trial and sentenced him to death. Plato turned to philosophy instead. Around 383 BCE he founded the Academy in Athens, where the young Aristotle came to study. He died in Athens around 347 BCE.
What he cared about

Plato wrote dialogues, not treatises, and Socrates is the main speaker in almost all of them. Their big questions:

- **The examined life:** a life without questioning is not worth living.
- **Knowing what you don't know** is where wisdom begins.
- **Justice in the soul:** a good person is at peace with himself, with reason in charge.
- **The Forms:** behind the changing world we see stand perfect, unchanging ideas.
- **Love** as the longing for what we lack, and in the end for the good itself.
What might surprise you

Plato never speaks in his own voice. He lets Socrates and others argue, so readers still debate which views were truly his. He even had Socrates warn that writing weakens memory, in a book that has lasted 2,400 years.

He also tried to put philosophy into politics. Three times he travelled to Syracuse, in Sicily, hoping to guide its rulers. The first tyrant turned against him, and the second never became the philosopher king Plato hoped for. A scroll from Herculaneum, read in 2024, even suggests he was once sold into slavery on the island of Aegina.
Where to start reading
The *Apology*: Socrates' speech at his trial. Short, clear, and moving. Benjamin Jowett's 1871 translation is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Plato thoughts (#95–108, #135–143), including #95, #96, #105, #106, and #108

pages.title: Rabindranath Tagore
sections: Who he was

Tagore was born into a leading family in Calcutta and wrote his first poems at eight. He became a poet, novelist, playwright, composer, painter, and teacher, and one of the key figures of the Bengal Renaissance.

In 1901 he founded a school at Santiniketan, which later grew into Visva-Bharati University. In 1913, after his own English version of *Gitanjali* moved readers like W. B. Yeats, he became the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize. He wrote some two thousand songs; two of them are now the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
What he cared about

- **Love as the way to freedom:** we become free not by escaping the world, but by loving it.
- **The unity of all life,** drawn from the Upanishads: the self, nature, and the divine are one.
- **Education in nature,** with art, music, and open-air classes.
- **One humanity:** he was a fierce critic of nationalism, in India and abroad.
What might surprise you

King George V knighted him in 1915. Four years later, after troops under a British general fired on an unarmed crowd at Amritsar, killing hundreds, he gave the knighthood back in protest.

He wanted India free from British rule, yet he also argued with Gandhi, and sometimes criticised his campaigns. He travelled widely and met Einstein, Bergson, and H. G. Wells. At sixty, he also took up drawing and painting, and his works were shown across Europe.
Where to start reading
*Stray Birds* (1916): tiny poems, often a single line, published in English. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Tagore thoughts (#374–379, #385–400), from *Sadhana* and *Stray Birds*

pages.title: Ralph Waldo Emerson
sections: Who he was

Emerson was born in Boston in 1803, the son of a Unitarian minister, and entered Harvard at 14. He became a minister himself. His first wife, Ellen, died of tuberculosis after less than two years of marriage, and two of his brothers soon followed.

After Ellen's death he grew more openly at odds with the church and resigned from the ministry in 1832. His essay *Nature* (1836) launched the movement known as Transcendentalism, and he became the friend and mentor of Henry David Thoreau.

He earned his living as a lecturer, giving some 1,500 talks across America, and turned many of them into essays. In his last decade his memory failed. He died in 1882, aged 78.
What he cared about

Emerson believed each person has direct access to truth, if they dare to trust it. His themes:

- **Self-reliance:** trust yourself, and don't let conformity silence your inner voice.
- **Freedom to change your mind:** a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.
- **Your own thoughts:** in great works we recognise ideas we once had and dismissed.
- **Compensation:** every gain has a cost, and every loss a hidden gain.
- **Inner peace:** only living by your own principles brings it.
What might surprise you

He shocked Harvard. In 1838 he told its divinity students that Jesus was a great man but not God. The address caused such a storm that the university did not invite him back to speak for 30 years.

He was also a quiet but firm opponent of slavery. He disliked the public eye, yet he lectured against it, denounced the Fugitive Slave Act, and welcomed the abolitionist John Brown to his home. Nietzsche called him "the most gifted of the Americans".
Where to start reading
"Self-Reliance" (1841): one essay, about an hour's read, full of lines worth keeping. Free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Ralph Waldo Emerson"
The app's Emerson thoughts (#261–265, #305–306), from "Self-Reliance" and "Compensation" (1841)

pages.title: René Descartes
sections: Who he was

Descartes was born in 1596 in Touraine, in France. His mother died when he was a year old. He was a sickly child, studied with the Jesuits at La Flèche, and took a law degree to please his father.

Instead of practising law, he joined the Dutch army as a volunteer to learn military engineering. One cold night in 1619, shut in a room heated by a stove, he had three dreams that he believed revealed a new philosophy to him.

He spent more than 20 years in the Dutch Republic and wrote all his major works there. In 1649 Queen Christina of Sweden invited him to her court. He died in Stockholm the next winter, probably of pneumonia.
What he cared about

Descartes wanted knowledge built on foundations so firm that nothing could shake them. His themes:

- **Doubt as a method:** accept nothing as true until you see clearly that it is.
- **I think, therefore I am:** even when doubting everything, he could not doubt that he was thinking.
- **Good sense, well used:** everyone has reason; what matters is how we direct it.
- **Master yourself:** change your desires rather than the order of the world.
- **Reading as conversation:** good books let us talk with the best minds of past ages.
What might surprise you

He was a great mathematician as well as a philosopher. He joined algebra and geometry, and the graph grid with x and y axes, the Cartesian coordinate system, is named after him. When Galileo was condemned in 1633, Descartes put his own book on the physical world in a drawer.

His private life was more ordinary than his reputation. With a servant, Helena Jans van der Strom, he had a daughter, Francine, who died of scarlet fever at five. In Sweden he was asked to teach the queen at 5 a.m. in a cold castle; they met only a few times and did not like each other.
Where to start reading
*Discourse on Method*: short, personal, and readable in an afternoon. John Veitch's translation (1850) is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Descartes thoughts (#180–183), from *Discourse on Method*, translated by John Veitch (1850)

pages.title: Rumi
sections: Who he was

Jalal al-Din Rumi was born to Persian parents in Wakhsh, in today's Tajikistan. While he was still a child, the advancing Mongols drove his family west, through Iran, Baghdad, and Damascus. At nineteen he settled with them in Konya, in today's Turkey, a land that had once been Roman, which is where his name, "the Roman", comes from.

Like his father, he became a respected Islamic scholar and teacher. Then, in 1244, he met a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, and his life changed. The two became inseparable. When Shams mysteriously disappeared, Rumi's grief poured out as poetry, and he kept writing until his death in Konya in 1273.
What he cared about

- **Love** as the force that moves everything, above all the longing of the soul for God.
- **Separation and longing:** the Masnavi opens with a reed flute, his favourite instrument, singing of separation.
- **Stories that teach:** his long poem, the *Masnavi*, is full of fables and everyday scenes.
- **Music and movement** as ways to reach the divine.
What might surprise you

Rumi is often called the world's most popular poet, and in recent years he has been one of the best-selling poets in the United States. But many popular English versions are free interpretations, not close translations of the Persian.

The famous whirling dervishes grew out of his teaching: after his death, his son and followers founded the Mevlevi order. When Rumi died, Christians and Jews joined the Muslims of Konya in the crowd that mourned him.
Where to start reading
The *Masnavi*, Book I, which opens with the song of the reed. E. H. Whinfield's 1898 abridged translation is free online.
sources: The app's Rumi thoughts (#555–559, #562–566, #593–597, #603–604), from the *Masnavi* and the *Divani Shamsi Tabriz*

pages.title: Sa'di
sections: Who he was

Sa'di was born in Shiraz, in southern Persia. His father, who taught him and, it is said, a lifelong habit of tolerance, died while Sa'di was still a boy. As a teenager he left for Baghdad to study, and then spent nearly thirty years travelling across the Islamic world.

He came home to Shiraz in 1257, already famous for his poems. He lived through the Mongol conquests: he wrote laments for the fall of Baghdad in 1258, and also a poem honouring the new Mongol rulers. Persians still call him simply "the Master".
What he cared about

His two great books, the *Bustan* (*The Orchard*) and the *Gulistan* (*The Rose Garden*), teach through short stories, many from the lives of kings, beggars, and travellers. Their lessons:

- **We are one family:** all people share one origin, so another's pain is our own.
- **Rulers serve the people,** as a shepherd serves his flock, not the other way round.
- **Contentment** is the only treasure worth asking for.
- **Patience** is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.
- **A kind lie** can be better than a truth that stirs up harm.
What might surprise you

Many of his stories are told in the first person, as adventures of his own: being taken prisoner by the Crusaders in Syria, or even killing a temple priest in India. Scholars think many of these are unlikely, and probably invented or told as if by himself for effect.

He also travelled far in Western memory. Voltaire loved the *Gulistan* and liked his friends to call him "Sa'di", and the lines on all humans as one family hang on a carpet in the United Nations building in New York.
Where to start reading
The *Gulistan*, chapter I, "On the Manners of Kings". Short stories with a lesson, in prose and verse. James Ross's translation, revised in 1900, is free online.
sources: The app's Sa'di thoughts (#573–576, #587–592), from the *Gulistan*

pages.title: Sei Shōnagon
pages.era: Japan, from the Heian court to the age of the samurai
sections: Who she was

Sei Shōnagon served as a lady-in-waiting to the Empress Teishi around the year 1000, at the Heian court in Kyoto. We do not know her real name. "Sei" comes from the family name of her father, the poet Kiyohara Motosuke, and "Shōnagon" is a court title whose link to her is unclear.

During her years at court she kept the notes that became *The Pillow Book*, finished around 1002. The Empress died in 1000, and after that the records of Sei Shōnagon almost vanish.

One tradition says she remarried and had a daughter. Another says she ended her days poor, as a Buddhist nun. We do not know which is true.
What she cared about

*The Pillow Book* mixes stories, poems, opinions, and about 164 lists, with headings like "Cheerful Things" or "Dreary Things". Her themes:

- **Small things with big feelings:** a withered flower or an old letter can bring back a whole past.
- **The seasons:** each has its own perfect moment, like spring at dawn or winter snow.
- **Taste:** she judges everything, from good letter paper to bad manners, with total confidence.
- **Honest dislikes:** she lists what annoys her as freely as what delights her.
- **Noticing:** the joy of paying close attention to an ordinary day.
