What might surprise you

She meant the book to be private. According to the story, she left it on a cushion she put out for a guest, who carried it off despite her pleas. It went on to shape a whole Japanese genre, *zuihitsu*, or "assorted writing".

Not everyone liked her. Her rival Murasaki Shikibu, author of *The Tale of Genji*, wrote about her sharply in her diary while admitting her gifts. Many readers still find her arrogant, and many love her sharp wit for exactly the same reason.
Where to start reading
The passages W. G. Aston translated in *A History of Japanese Literature* (1899): a short taste of her lists, free online. For the whole book, look for a modern complete translation.
sources: The app's Sei Shōnagon thoughts (#542–545, #548–549), from *The Pillow Book*, translated by W. G. Aston (1899)

pages.title: Seneca
pages.era: Rome, from the Republic to its fall
sections: Who he was

Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born in Corduba, in Roman Spain, and grew up in Rome. He became a well-known speaker and writer. In 41 CE he was exiled to Corsica on an adultery charge that many historians doubt.

Eight years later, Agrippina brought him back to teach her son, the future emperor Nero. When Nero came to power in 54, Seneca became one of his closest advisers and, for some years, one of the most powerful men in Rome. He stepped back around 62. In 65, after a plot against Nero failed, the emperor ordered him to take his own life, although his part in the plot is unlikely.
What he cared about

For Seneca, philosophy was a cure for the mind, not a theory. He wrote less for the perfect wise person than for people still trying to improve. His key ideas:

- **Time** is our only real possession, and we waste it.
- **Anger** and other strong emotions come from our own judgments, so reason can calm them.
- **Death** is a natural law, and thinking about it helps us live well now.
- **Each evening**, look back on your day honestly, without harshness.
What might surprise you

Seneca praised a simple life while being one of the richest men in Rome, partly through money lending. Critics in his own time attacked him for it; he answered that wealth is fine if you do not depend on it.

He also served Nero, and one of his essays praises the young emperor's mercy. Readers still argue about whether he was a hypocrite or someone who saw his own weaknesses clearly. Some of his remarks about women also reflect the views of his time.
Where to start reading

*On the Shortness of Life*: short, clear, and still sharp. Then the *Letters to Lucilius*, 124 letters written in his last years. Aubrey Stewart's translation is free on Project Gutenberg. His tragedies, such as *Medea* and *Thyestes*, later influenced Shakespeare.

pages.title: Simone Weil
pages.era: Europe in the age of world wars
sections: Who she was

Weil was born in Paris into an agnostic Jewish family from Alsace; her elder brother André became a famous mathematician. At school her radical opinions earned her the nickname "the Red Virgin". She became a philosophy teacher, taking breaks for poor health and for political work.

She wanted to know the lives of working people from the inside. She took a year off teaching to work, unknown, on factory lines, including at Renault. In 1936 she joined anarchist fighters in the Spanish Civil War, until she badly burned herself in a pot of boiling cooking oil and had to leave.
What she cared about

Weil wrote about suffering, justice, and attention, and she grew more and more drawn to Christian mysticism. In the essay the app reads, on the right use of school studies, she argues:

- **Attention** is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
- **Those who suffer** need, above all, someone able to pay attention to them.
- **No real effort of attention is ever lost,** even when it seems to fail.
- **Intelligence grows in joy,** and is led by desire, not by force.
What might surprise you

She was drawn to Christianity yet long refused baptism, believing that such a step had to come from God, not from her own decision. She may have been baptized only in her last months.

During the Second World War she worked for the Free French in London. Ill with tuberculosis, she refused to eat more than people in occupied France, and died of heart failure in 1943, at 34. Almost all her books were published after her death, and later inspired writers from Albert Camus to Iris Murdoch.
Where to start reading
"Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God": a short essay on attention. The app uses its own translation of the French.

pages.title: Swami Vivekananda
sections: Who he was

Vivekananda was born Narendranath Datta into a well-off family in Calcutta, the son of a lawyer. As a young man he was drawn to a reform movement that rejected caste barriers. At eighteen he met the mystic Ramakrishna, became his closest disciple, and later took the vows of a monk.

After Ramakrishna's death he spent five years walking across India, living on alms, and saw for himself the poverty of millions under British rule. In 1893 he sailed to Chicago for the Parliament of the World's Religions. Back in India, he founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897, devoted to education and social service. He died in 1902, aged 39.
What he cared about

The app reads his *Karma-Yoga* (1896), lectures on the path of action:

- **Work without attachment:** act fully, but do not cling to the results.
- **Misery comes from attachment,** not from work itself.
- **Do good because it is good,** not for money, fame, or reward.
- **Giving blesses the giver:** in helping the world, we help ourselves.
- **Teach yourself:** no one is ever really taught by another.
What might surprise you

His Chicago speech, which opened with the words "Sisters and brothers of America", called for religious tolerance and is still remembered today. He went on to lecture in the United States and England, and two American universities offered him academic posts.

He was a monk, yet he urged practical action: schools, relief work, and service to the poor. Today his birthday, 12 January, is celebrated in India as National Youth Day.
Where to start reading
*Karma-Yoga*, chapter 3, "The Secret of Work". Short lectures in plain English, free online.

pages.title: The Bhagavad Gita
sections: What this text is

The *Bhagavad Gita*, "the Song of God", is a poem of 700 verses in 18 chapters, set inside the great Indian epic, the *Mahabharata*. Tradition credits it to the sage Vyasa; scholars think several authors probably shaped it.

It is a dialogue on a battlefield. The prince Arjuna sees relatives, friends, and teachers in the enemy army, drops his bow, and does not want to fight. His charioteer, Krishna, whom Hindu tradition sees as a form of the god Vishnu, answers his doubts. Among Hindu traditions, it is the most widely revered sacred text.
What it cares about

- **Act without clinging to results:** your concern is the action, never its fruits.
- **Do your own duty,** even imperfectly, rather than someone else's well.
- **A steady mind:** stay calm in pleasure and pain, success and failure.
- **The self as friend:** raise yourself by yourself; your own self can be your best friend or your enemy.
- **Moderation:** neither too much nor too little, in food, sleep, or effort.
What might surprise you

Readers have argued for a long time about its setting. Some read it literally, as a call to fight; others, including Emerson and Walt Whitman, read the battle as a picture of the struggle inside each person. Gandhi learned verses of its second chapter by heart and called them a companion in his non-violent movement.

Its first English translation appeared in 1785. In 1965, J. Robert Oppenheimer, who had led the making of the atomic bomb, recited a verse from it in a television documentary.
Where to start reading
Chapter II, which sums up the whole teaching. Kashinath Trimbak Telang's 1882 translation and Edwin Arnold's verse version, *The Song Celestial* (1885), are free online.

pages.title: The Dhammapada
header: sayings of the Buddha, 5th century BCE
sections: What this text is

The *Dhammapada* is a collection of sayings of the Buddha in verse, and one of the most widely read Buddhist texts in the world. It has 423 short verses, grouped by theme into 26 chapters, such as thought, anger, happiness, and old age.

It belongs to the Pali Canon, the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism. Tradition holds that the Buddha spoke each verse on a particular occasion, in answer to something that had happened in his community. The title joins two words: *dhamma*, the teaching, and *pada*, path or verse.
What it cares about

- **The mind comes first:** what we think shapes what we become.
- **Hatred never ends hatred;** love does.
- **Self-mastery:** conquering yourself is greater than conquering others.
- **Watchfulness:** "earnestness" in Müller's words: stay awake, and do not drift.
- **Kindness:** everyone fears pain and death, just as we do.
What might surprise you

The verses are short, but they came with stories. A later commentary, linked to the scholar Buddhaghosa, gives the event behind each verse, and it is a rich source of legends about the Buddha's life.

Many verses work by contrast: joy and suffering, good and bad action, truth and lies, side by side. The *Dhammapada* is a religious text, and the app reads it here as practical wisdom that anyone can test.
Where to start reading

Read a chapter at a time, in any order; the chapters on thought and on anger are good first steps. F. Max Müller's 1881 translation, made for the series *Sacred Books of the East*, is free on Project Gutenberg.
sources: The app's Dhammapada thoughts (#307–336 and others), from Müller's translation

pages.title: The Questions of King Milinda
sections: What this text is

*The Questions of King Milinda* (in Pali, *Milindapañha*) is a Buddhist book in the form of a dialogue. A king asks hard questions about Buddhist teaching, and a monk named Nāgasena answers them, often with a simple image.

The king is real. Milinda is the Indian name of Menander I, a Greek king who ruled a large realm in what is now Pakistan and northwest India in the 2nd century BCE. Nāgasena is known only from this book and from later legend.

Scholars agree the work grew over time. Its earliest part was probably written between 100 BCE and 200 CE, and later authors added more. In Myanmar it is part of the Buddhist canon; in Thailand and Sri Lanka it is not.
What it cares about

The king wants clear reasons, not just faith, and the monk gives them. Its themes:

- **No fixed self:** a chariot is not its wheels, pole, or axle; "chariot" is a name for parts working together, and so is a person.
- **Rebirth without a soul:** how can something be reborn if there is no lasting self to carry over?
- **Responsibility:** how our deeds follow us, and whether doing wrong knowingly is worse than doing it unknowingly.
- **Puzzles in the teaching:** dozens of apparent contradictions in Buddhist texts, taken one by one.
- **Teaching by image:** hard ideas made clear through everyday comparisons.
What might surprise you

A Greek and an Indian sit down to argue philosophy. Yet scholars note that the dialogue shows little sign of Greek thought; its ideas trace back to Indian sources such as the Upanishads.

Buddhist tradition says the king was won over, handed his kingdom to his son, and left the world. A Greek source, Plutarch, says instead that he died in camp on campaign and that his cities shared out his ashes. Its 1890 translator, T. W. Rhys Davids, called it "the masterpiece of Indian prose".
Where to start reading
Book II, the chariot dialogue: a few pages that sum up the Buddhist idea of the self. T. W. Rhys Davids's 1890 translation, in the *Sacred Books of the East*, is free online.
sources: The app's thought from this text (#355), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1890)

pages.title: The Upanishads
sections: What these texts are

The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts that close the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. Earlier parts of the Vedas deal with hymns and rituals; the Upanishads turn inward, to meditation, consciousness, and the nature of reality. The name is often explained as "sitting down near": a student sitting by a teacher to receive knowledge.

About 108 are known. The dozen or so oldest, called the principal Upanishads, were passed down by heart for centuries. The *Brihadaranyaka* is among the most ancient. The app also reads the *Katha*, *Isha*, and *Mundaka*, composed probably in the last few centuries BCE.
What they care about

- **The self and the whole:** the deepest self (*Atman*) and ultimate reality (*Brahman*) are closely linked, and in many readings one.
- **The good and the pleasant** are two different things, and the wise choose the good.
- **The self as a rider:** the body is the chariot, the intellect the driver, the senses the horses.
- **We become our desires:** as a person desires, so he acts, and so he becomes.
- **Seeing all beings in oneself,** and oneself in all beings.
What might surprise you

They reached Europe by a long road. In 1656, the Mughal prince Dara Shukoh had fifty of them translated from Sanskrit into Persian. A French scholar then turned the Persian into Latin, and that Latin version is what Schopenhauer read. He called them the most rewarding and uplifting reading in the world.

One of the last things the poet W. B. Yeats published, in 1938, was a translation of ten principal Upanishads.
Where to start reading

The *Katha Upanishad*: short, and built around a story: a boy, Nachiketa, meets Yama, the god of death in Hindu tradition, and asks him about the self. F. Max Müller's translation, in the *Sacred Books of the East*, is free online.
sources: The app's Upanishad thoughts (#363–367, #373, #409), from the *Katha*, *Isha*, *Brihadaranyaka*, and *Mundaka*

pages.title: Thomas Hobbes
sections: Who he was

Hobbes was born in 1588 in Wiltshire, England, early, it was said, because his mother took fright at news of the Spanish Armada. He later joked that she gave birth to twins: himself and fear. His father left the family after a fight, and a wealthy uncle raised him.

After Oxford he became tutor to the Cavendish family, which gave him a living, a library, and travels across Europe. An early biographer says he met Galileo. He translated Thucydides into English straight from the Greek.

As England slid into civil war, he left for Paris in 1640 and stayed until 1651. There he taught mathematics to the exiled young Prince of Wales and wrote *Leviathan* (1651). He lived to 91, still writing, and was said to have called death "a great leap in the dark".
What he cared about

Hobbes asked why people obey rulers at all, and what happens when they stop. His themes:

- **The state of nature:** without government, life is a war of all against all, "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short".
- **The social contract:** people agree to give up some freedom to a ruler in exchange for safety.
- **A strong sovereign:** after the horrors of civil war, he thought only a powerful ruler could keep the peace.
- **Peace makes thought possible:** leisure is the mother of philosophy, and an ordered state the mother of peace.
- **Fear and self-interest:** he saw them as the real drivers of human behaviour.
What might surprise you

His view of people sounds bleak, but his argument is modern: political power comes from the people's agreement, not from God or birth. That made him enemies on all sides, and he was often accused of atheism.

He also kept working late into old age. In his mid-eighties he published an English translation of Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.
Where to start reading
*Leviathan*, chapters 13 to 17: the state of nature and the birth of the state. Free on Project Gutenberg.

pages.title: Vauvenargues
sections: Who he was

Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues, was born in Aix-en-Provence in 1715, into a noble but poor family. Frail health kept his schooling to a minimum: he never learned Latin or Greek. He joined the army as a young man.

In 1742 he took part in the disastrous siege of Prague. During the winter retreat his legs froze, and he never fully recovered. Hoping for a career as a diplomat, he wrote for two years to ministers and even to King Louis XV, with no success.

Then smallpox left him disfigured, nearly blind, and with a chronic cough. He moved to Paris in 1745 and lived almost alone, seeing a few friends, Voltaire among them. He published his only book in 1746, without his name, and died the next year, aged 31.
What he cared about

His book gathered an essay on the human mind with hundreds of short reflections and maxims. His themes:

- **The heart thinks too:** great thoughts come from the heart, and reason follows.
- **Living, not fearing death:** the thought of death deceives us when it makes us forget to live.
- **Patience:** he called it the art of hoping.
- **Acting, not only reflecting:** no one makes more mistakes than those who act only after reflection.
- **A good view of people:** where others saw only self-interest, he saw real nobility.
What might surprise you

He was the friend Voltaire admired, though Voltaire was 20 years older and already famous. Voltaire encouraged him to publish and urged him to bring out an improved second edition.

He is often set beside La Rochefoucauld, but they look at people from opposite sides. La Rochefoucauld finds vanity behind every virtue. Vauvenargues thinks well of human beings and has been called a modern Stoic. His name only appeared on his work in 1797, and his maxims became popular in the 1850s, a century after his death.
Where to start reading
*Reflections and Maxims*: short lines you can open anywhere. Free in French on Wikisource; the app uses its own translations.
sources: Encyclopædia Britannica, "Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues"
Wikipedia, "Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues"
The app's Vauvenargues thoughts (#631–633), from *Reflections and Maxims*

pages.title: Voltaire
sections: Who he was

Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet in Paris, was educated by the Jesuits. His sharp tongue got him into trouble early: a satirical verse about the regent earned him eleven months in the Bastille, and he was later sent into exile in England, where he admired English freedoms and Newton's science.

From 1733 he lived for years with Émilie du Châtelet at Cirey. He spent time at the court of Frederick the Great of Prussia, and later settled at Ferney, near Geneva, on the French border, safely out of reach of the French king. He died in 1778, at 83.
What he cared about

Voltaire wrote plays, histories, tales, and thousands of letters, always with wit. His causes:

- **Tolerance:** we are all weak and wrong, so let us forgive one another.
- **Freedom of speech and religion,** and the separation of church and state.
- **Against fanaticism:** he urged his friends to "crush the infamous", the abuses of church and crown.
- **Against easy optimism:** in *Candide* (1759) he mocked the idea that all is for the best.
- **Justice:** better to risk saving a guilty person than to condemn an innocent one.
What might surprise you

From 1762 he used his fame to defend victims of injustice. The most famous was Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant tortured to death on the charge of killing his son to stop him becoming a Catholic. Voltaire took up the case and wrote his *Treatise on Tolerance* about it.

The champion of tolerance also had blind spots. He wrote with open hostility about Jews, and he supported the theory that human races had separate origins. Some historians link these views to his investments in colonial companies involved in the slave trade, though he also mocked slavery in *Candide*.
Where to start reading
*Candide*: short, fast, and still funny. Free on Project Gutenberg in several translations; the app uses its own.
sources: The app's Voltaire thoughts (#611–616), from *Candide*, *Zadig*, and the *Philosophical Dictionary*

pages.title: William James
sections: Who he was

James was born in New York into a wealthy, unusual family: his father was a religious thinker, his brother Henry became a great novelist, and his sister Alice a diarist. He trained as a doctor at Harvard but never practised. In 1865 he joined a scientific expedition up the Amazon.

He went on to teach at Harvard, where he gave the first psychology course in the United States, and is often called the father of American psychology. With Charles Sanders Peirce, he also founded the philosophy known as pragmatism. Students remembered him for his kindness and lack of arrogance.
What he cared about

James asked what difference an idea makes in real life. His themes:

- **Is life worth living?** Yes, if we are willing to act and take risks without guarantees.
- **Need and struggle** bring us alive; triumph often leaves a void.
- **The right to believe:** on some questions, we must choose before all the evidence is in.
- **Ideals and "over-beliefs"** are the most interesting thing about a person.
- **The stream of consciousness:** the mind flows, it does not come in neat pieces.
What might surprise you

The philosopher of hope knew despair from the inside. As a young man he went through long periods of depression and poor health. In 1870, reading the French philosopher Charles Renouvier, he decided to believe in his own free will, and he later called that day a crisis in his life.

His idea of a "stream of consciousness" travelled far beyond psychology: it shaped modernist writers such as James Joyce.
Where to start reading
"Is Life Worth Living?", an essay in *The Will to Believe* (1897). Short, direct, and free online.
sources: The app's William James thoughts (#239–242), from *The Will to Believe*

pages.title: Zhuangzi
sections: Who he was

Zhuang Zhou, called Zhuangzi ("Master Zhuang"), came from the town of Meng in the state of Song. He lived during the Warring States period, a time of war and of many rival schools of thought, and was a contemporary of Mencius.

We know very little about his life. The historian Sima Qian says he held a minor official post and turned down a high position offered by the king of Chu because he valued his freedom. Most other stories about him come from the book that carries his name.
What he cared about

Zhuangzi doubted that any single point of view can hold the whole truth. Each of us sees from where we stand, like the frog at the bottom of a well. His main ideas:

- **The Way** (Dao) cannot be fully known or put into words, and it is always changing.
- **Flexible minds** do better than fixed ones: stop clinging to one view and respond to what is in front of you.
- **Skill** at its best feels effortless, like the cook whose knife never goes dull.
- **The useless** can thrive: the tree nobody wants to cut down grows old.
- **Death** is part of nature's constant change, not something to fear.
What might surprise you

Zhuangzi probably did not write most of the book. Only the first seven chapters, the Inner Chapters, are usually credited to him; the rest came from later followers with quite different views.

He is also funny. He puts words in the mouth of Confucius, Taoism's great rival, and lets him say Taoist things. When his wife died, a friend found him drumming on a pot and singing, and was shocked. Even an ancient chapter of the book criticises him for ignoring practical matters.
Where to start reading

The Inner Chapters, especially chapter 2 (with the butterfly dream) and chapter 3 (the cook). Short, strange, and full of stories. The translations by Herbert Giles (1889) and James Legge (1891) are free online.
sources: The app's thoughts #433 and #437 (Zhuangzi, ch. 5 and 18, Giles translation)

pages.title: Émilie du Châtelet
sections: Who she was

Émilie du Châtelet was born in Paris into a noble family. Her father let her discuss astronomy with the writer Fontenelle when she was ten, and by twelve she read Latin, Italian, Greek, and German. She married a marquis at eighteen; after three children, the couple agreed to live separate lives.

From 1733 she studied mathematics with leading scientists, and from 1734 she lived with Voltaire at Cirey, her family's country house, where they set up a laboratory. In 1738 she secretly entered a science prize of the Académie des Sciences on the nature of fire. Her essay was published by the Académie, the first work by a woman it printed.
What she cared about

She wanted to understand how the world works, and to give physics solid foundations. Her main work:

- **Foundations of Physics** (1740) tried to bring together the ideas of Newton and Leibniz.
- **Energy:** she argued that a moving body's force grows with the square of its speed, a key step towards the modern idea of energy.
- **Newton's Principia:** her French translation, with commentary, is still the standard one.
- **Happiness:** in her *Discourse on Happiness*, she says we need passions we can satisfy and freedom from prejudice, and that the love of study is the most reliable source of joy.
What might surprise you

For a long time, history remembered her mainly as Voltaire's partner, not as a scientist in her own right. Only in recent decades have scholars judged her work on its own terms.

She was also a keen gambler: once she lost a large sum in one evening at court, to card cheats. At 42 she became pregnant, feared she would not survive, and kept working to finish her Newton translation. She died six days after giving birth.
Where to start reading
The *Discourse on Happiness*: short, personal, and honest. She wrote it in the 1740s, and it was only published in 1779, thirty years after her death. The French original is free on Wikisource.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Émilie du Châtelet"
Project Vox, *Discours sur le bonheur* (1779 edition)

pages.title: Beauty and art
sections: The question in one line
Is beauty out there, or in the eye of the beholder?
How the traditions see it

**Kenkō and Okakura (Japanese Aesthetics).** The Japanese writers love what is unfinished. Kenkō thought it better to leave a little imperfection, since perfect uniformity is dull. In *The Book of Tea*, Okakura says true beauty is found by the one who completes the incomplete in their own mind: what is left unsaid gives the viewer a part to play.

**Hume (Enlightenment Ethics).** Hume started from the view that beauty is no quality in things, but exists in the mind that looks at them. Yet he did not leave it there. Some judgements are better than others, he argued, and the standard of taste is the shared verdict of rare, experienced, unprejudiced critics. Studying beauty, he added, softens the temper.

**Laozi (Taoism).** The *Tao Te Ching* sees a hidden cost in naming beauty: as soon as everyone knows what is beautiful, they also know what is ugly. Each idea brings its opposite with it.

**Nietzsche and Emerson (Existential Thought, Humanists and Essayists).** For Nietzsche, the greatest art is to "give style" to your own character, shaping strengths and weaknesses into one whole. Emerson saw in every work of genius our own rejected thoughts, coming back to us with a kind of borrowed majesty.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them link beauty to the person who sees it, not only to the object. They differ on how far. Hume searches for a standard that lets us say some tastes are better; the Japanese writers make the viewer a partner in the work; Nietzsche turns the art inward, onto how we shape our lives.
sources: The app's thoughts #177, #188, #259, #264, #421, #525, #533, and #534, with their sources

pages.title: Change and impermanence
sections: The question in one line
Everything changes, so how should we live with it?
How the traditions see it

**Heraclitus and Lucretius (Classical Greek Philosophy, Epicureanism).** Heraclitus said you cannot step into the same river twice, because new water is always flowing. Lucretius saw the same motion in matter itself: nothing comes from nothing, and nothing returns to nothing; things only break apart and form again.

**The Dhammapada (Buddhist Philosophy).** For the *Dhammapada*, seeing clearly that all created things pass away is itself a path out of suffering. We suffer when we cling to what cannot last.

**Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius (Stoicism).** Epictetus advised never saying "I have lost it", only "I have given it back": a child, a wife, an estate were only lent to us. Marcus Aurelius put it in five words: the universe is transformation.

**Kenkō and Okakura (Japanese Aesthetics).** The Japanese writers find beauty in passing things. Kenkō asks whether we should look at the moon only when it is full, or at flowers only in full bloom. Okakura invites us to "dream of evanescence".
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them start from the same fact: nothing stays as it is. They differ on what to do with it. The Stoics accept it calmly; the Buddhist texts let go; the Japanese writers find beauty in it; Nietzsche goes further and welcomes change as the way we become new.
sources: The app's thoughts #18, #33, #88, #121, #209, #345, #515, #517, and #529, with their sources

pages.title: Character and virtue
sections: The question in one line
What makes a person good, and can you become one?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Virtue, for Aristotle, is a settled trait of character, and you build it the way you learn a craft: by doing. We become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. Each virtue sits between two extremes, like courage between cowardice and recklessness. Hitting that middle point is hard, and it takes practical wisdom.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** People start out much alike, Confucius said, and practice makes them grow far apart. The ideal is the "superior man", who asks a lot of himself and little of others, and who leads by example rather than by orders. Virtue is never lonely: whoever practises it will find neighbours.

**The Dhammapada (Buddhist Philosophy).** The *Dhammapada* puts the work in each person's hands: by oneself evil is done, and by oneself it is left undone. Small good acts add up, like a water jar filling drop by drop. Anger is overcome by love, and evil by good.

**Kant (Enlightenment Ethics).** Kant moved the focus from character to the will. Talents, courage, and even happiness can be used for bad ends; only a good will is good without qualification. Morality, he said, is not about how to be happy, but how to become worthy of happiness.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All four say goodness takes effort and is not simply given at birth. They split on where it lives. For Aristotle and Confucius, it is a character shaped by long practice and good company; for Kant, it is the intention behind each act, done out of duty. Virtue ethics, the tradition of Aristotle and Confucius, faded in the West after the Enlightenment and returned in the late 1950s.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Kant's Moral Philosophy"

pages.title: Death and mortality
sections: The question in one line
Should we think about death, and can we stop fearing it?
How the traditions see it

**Epicurus and Lucretius (Epicureanism).** Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us: where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. Lucretius asked why we should not leave life like a guest leaving a banquet, full and content. On the day he died, in great pain, Epicurus wrote to a friend that the memory of their conversations outweighed it all.

**Marcus Aurelius and Montaigne (Stoicism, Humanists and Essayists).** Marcus Aurelius reminded himself not to act as if he had ten thousand years. Montaigne took an old saying for an essay title: to study philosophy is to learn to die. Whoever has learned to die, he said, has unlearned how to be a slave.

**Zhuangzi (Taoism).** When Zhuangzi's wife died, a friend found him beating on a bowl and singing. He had grieved like anyone, he explained, then saw her death as one more change, like spring turning to summer, autumn, and winter. Tagore says something close: death belongs to life as birth does.

**Omar Khayyam and Kenkō (Persian and Sufi Poetry, Japanese Aesthetics).** For Khayyam, death is a door with no key and a veil no one sees past, so we should make the most of the days we have. Kenkō notes that death does not wait its turn like the seasons; it presses on us from behind.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most of them say that facing death honestly makes life clearer and fear smaller. They split on how much to think about it. Montaigne and the Stoics advise keeping it in mind; Spinoza answered that a free person thinks of death least of all, and that wisdom is a meditation on life.
sources: The app's thoughts #4, #59, #73, #75, #170, #277, #387, #437, #520, #582, and #583, with their sources

pages.title: Democracy
sections: The question in one line
Should the people rule, and what keeps the many from going wrong?
How the traditions see it

**Athens and Plato (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Democracy began in Athens around 508 BCE. Citizens voted directly in an assembly, and many officials and jurors were chosen by lot. But only adult male citizens took part, perhaps one person in five or fewer: women, slaves, and foreigners were left out.

Plato did not trust it. In his parable of the ship, the sailors fight over the helm, while the true pilot, who knows the winds and the stars, is mocked as a stargazer. He had seen a democratic jury sentence his teacher Socrates to death in 399 BCE.

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Aristotle was more open. A citizen, for him, is someone who takes turns governing and being governed, and a crowd can judge many things better than one person. Still, he feared rule by the many could turn into mob rule. He preferred a mixed government, held steady by a strong middle class.

**Laozi (Taoism).** The *Tao Te Ching* looks at power from below. The best rulers are those the people hardly notice; worse ones are loved, then feared, then despised. Good government works quietly and lets people feel they did things themselves.

**Rousseau and Mill (Enlightenment Ethics).** Rousseau put the people at the heart of the state: when citizens stop caring about public affairs, the state is lost. Mill, a century later, saw a new danger. A majority can be a tyrant too, and silencing even one person who disagrees harms everyone. The phrase "tyranny of the majority" comes from Alexis de Tocqueville; Mill made it famous.
Where they agree, and where they don't

None of them trusts power without limits, whoever holds it. They split on whether ordinary people can be trusted to judge. Plato said no, Aristotle said often, and Mill said yes, but only with free speech protecting the few who disagree.

pages.title: Desire and simplicity
sections: The question in one line
Would we be happier wanting less?
How the traditions see it

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** Epicurus sorted desires into three kinds: natural and necessary, like drinking when thirsty; natural but not necessary, like costly food; and neither, like statues in your honour. The first are easy to satisfy; the last have no limit. Nature's wealth, he said, is small and easy to get.

**Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, and Seneca (Stoicism).** Marcus Aurelius advised doing few things if you want peace of mind. Epictetus put it more bluntly: don't admire your clothes, and you won't be angry with the thief. Seneca noted that we fear everything as if we were mortal, and want everything as if we would live forever.

**The Bhagavad Gita and the Dhammapada (Indian Philosophy, Buddhist Philosophy).** The *Gita* traces a chain: dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. Its answer is to act without clinging to the fruits of action. The *Dhammapada* says there is no fire like passion.

**Laozi and Thoreau (Taoism, Humanists and Essayists).** For Laozi, there is no greater calamity than never being content. Many centuries later, Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond to keep only the essentials of life. His advice: "Simplify, simplify."
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most agree that endless wanting makes us unhappy, and that it is better to change our desires than the world. Not everyone wants to drop desire, though. Émilie du Châtelet wrote that we are happy only through tastes and passions that are satisfied, and Simone Weil saw desire as what leads the mind.

pages.title: Duty
sections: The question in one line
Should we do what is right even when we don't feel like it, and even when it costs us?
How the traditions see it

**Kant (Enlightenment Ethics).** For Kant, nothing is good without condition except a good will. An act has moral worth only when it is done from duty, out of respect for the moral law, not from feeling or for the results. That law comes from reason itself, and it commands without conditions: Kant calls it the categorical imperative. Because every person has this reason, every person has equal worth and deserves equal respect.

**The Stoics (Stoicism).** The Stoics spoke of *kathekon*, the fitting or proper action: what our nature and our roles call for, as parents, citizens, or friends. Cicero's *On Duties*, one of the most read books of Roman ethics, is built on this idea. Marcus Aurelius put it shortly: stop talking about what a good person should be, and be one.

**Confucius and Mencius (Confucianism).** In Confucian ethics, duty lives in relationships: to parents, rulers, friends, and strangers. Righteousness, *yi*, is one of the five qualities of the gentleman, beside benevolence, ritual, wisdom, and trustworthiness. Mencius said a person should simply not do what their own sense of righteousness forbids.

**The Bhagavad Gita (Indian Philosophy).** The Gita speaks of *svadharma*, your own duty, set by your nature and place in life. Arjuna must fight, because that is his duty as a warrior, but without craving the fruits of his action. (See also *Karma and dharma*.)
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them say duty is not just a feeling we wait for. They disagree on where it comes from. For Kant, it comes from reason, the same for everyone. For the Stoics and Confucius, it comes from our nature and our roles. For the Gita, it comes from our station, which in its world was tied to birth. Mill, by contrast, saw the inner pull of duty as a feeling in our own mind, trained by upbringing. And in 1943 Simone Weil argued that duties come before rights: a right means something only when others are bound to respect it.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Kant's Moral Philosophy"

pages.title: Ego, pride, and humility
sections: The question in one line
How much should we think of ourselves?
How the traditions see it

**Laozi (Taoism).** The *Tao Te Ching* praises water: it helps everything and settles in the low places others avoid. A cup filled to the brim is hard to carry. Knowing others is clever, it says, but knowing yourself is wisdom.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Confucius did not worry about being unknown, only about not knowing others. He noted that people of old studied to improve themselves, while people of his day studied to be seen. His students said he was free of four things, among them stubbornness and egoism.

**Epictetus (Stoicism).** The first task of anyone who studies philosophy, said Epictetus, is to drop self-conceit, because nobody can learn what they think they already know. He also asked his students to remember how small a part of the whole they are.

**La Rochefoucauld and Erasmus (Humanists and Essayists).** La Rochefoucauld called self-love the greatest of flatterers, and saw it behind even our virtues. In Erasmus's *Praise of Folly*, Folly herself admits that nothing is sillier than admiring yourself.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see pride as a blind spot that keeps us from learning and from seeing others clearly. They differ on the cure. Laozi, Confucius, and Epictetus think practice can make us humbler. La Rochefoucauld doubts we ever fully escape self-love; at best we learn to notice it.
sources: The app's thoughts #23, #44, #290, #301, #410, #411, #415, #468, #483, and #490, with their sources

pages.title: Equality
sections: The question in one line
Are people equal, and equal in what?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Aristotle gave the basic rule of fairness: treat like cases alike. Citizens, for him, took turns ruling and being ruled. But he did not think all people were alike: in the same book he argued that some are slaves by nature, an idea later used to defend slavery.

**The Stoics and Confucius (Stoicism, Confucianism).** Other traditions stressed what we share. The Stoics taught the natural equality of all beings who have reason. Confucius said people are much alike by nature, and grow apart only by practice.

**Rousseau (Enlightenment Ethics).** Rousseau opens *The Social Contract* by saying people are born free, yet everywhere they are in chains. In his earlier *Discourse on Inequality*, he traced social inequality to the first fences around land: we are lost, he warned, if we forget that the fruits belong to all and the earth to no one.

**Wollstonecraft and Fuller (Enlightenment Ethics, Humanists and Essayists).** Both asked why equality stopped at men. Wollstonecraft argued that women seemed weaker only because they were denied education. Fuller noted that the self-reliance praised in her was called a fault in most women.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Until the 18th century, most thinkers assumed people were unequal by nature; the idea of natural rights changed that. Today most agree people are equal in dignity. The open question is equal in what: rights, chances, or results. Rousseau worried about unequal property; Aristotle, even with his blind spots, about treating like cases alike.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Jean Jacques Rousseau"
The app's thoughts listed above, with their sources

pages.title: Fortune
sections: The question in one line
When luck turns against us, should we accept it, or fight it?
How the traditions see it

**Epictetus and Seneca (Stoicism).** Epictetus began his handbook with one division: some things are in our power, and others are not. Our judgements, choices, and desires are ours; health, wealth, and reputation are not. Seneca drew the lesson: fortune can take away only what she gave.

**Boethius (Stoicism).** Boethius was a senior Roman official who lost everything and wrote in prison, waiting for death. In his *Consolation*, Philosophy herself visits him. She shows him that riches, status, power, and pleasure are only the goods of fortune, of little real worth, and that true happiness lies in virtue, which fortune cannot touch. Fortune turns her wheel, and complaining that it turns is foolish.

**Descartes (Enlightenment Ethics).** Descartes made the Stoic answer a rule for his own life: to try always to master himself rather than fortune, and to change his desires rather than the order of the world.

**Machiavelli (Humanists and Essayists).** Machiavelli saw *Fortuna* as the great enemy of political order. In *The Prince* he compares her to a river in flood that sweeps everything away. Yet floods can be prepared for: precautions taken in calm weather can turn aside the worst of the damage, and a ruler's skill, his *virtù*, lies in that preparation. In the same chapter he also wrote that fortune is a woman who must be beaten and mastered, an image that shocks readers today.
Where they agree, and where they don't

They all agree that much of life is out of our hands. They disagree on what to do about it. The Stoics, Boethius, and Descartes turn inward: change your desires, and fortune loses its hold. Machiavelli turns outward: prepare, act boldly, and win back some of what luck would take. Buddhism offers a third view: what happens to us may follow from past actions, but how we respond is still ours (see *Karma and dharma*).
sources: The app's thoughts listed above, with their sources

pages.title: Freedom
sections: The question in one line
Are you free when nobody stops you, or when you master yourself?
How the traditions see it

**The Stoics and the East: freedom inside.** Epictetus taught that some things are in our power and others are not; freedom starts with knowing the difference. Spinoza called being ruled by your emotions a kind of bondage. Confucius said an army can lose its general, but nobody can take away the will of an ordinary person. Here, freedom is something no prison can remove.

**Mill: freedom from others.** For Mill, the only freedom worth the name is to pursue your own good in your own way, as long as you do not stop others from doing the same. Over your own body and mind, you rule. Society may step in only to prevent harm to others. Yet Mill limited this to people "in the maturity of their faculties", and in the same chapter he called despotism legitimate over people he called "barbarians", if it improved them.

**Rousseau and Locke: freedom with others.** Rousseau opens *The Social Contract* by saying people are born free and everywhere in chains. His answer is not fewer laws, but laws the people make together. Locke agrees that law, done well, does not restrain freedom but protects and enlarges it.

**Wollstonecraft and Fuller: freedom for whom?** Both asked why freedom stopped at men. Wollstonecraft argued that blind obedience is what power wants, and education is the way out. Fuller wanted every path open to women as freely as to men.
Where they agree, and where they don't

In 1958 the philosopher Isaiah Berlin named the split: "negative" freedom, being left alone, and "positive" freedom, being in control of your own life. Mill stands for the first, Rousseau for the second. Berlin warned that the second can be abused, when rulers claim to force people towards their "real" good. Liberals, in turn, would not call the Stoics' inner freedom real freedom at all.

John Stuart Mill, *On Liberty* (1859), chapter I (Project Gutenberg)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2014 version of the same entry (on the Stoics)

pages.title: Friendship and kindness
sections: The question in one line
What makes someone a real friend, and why do we need them?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** He saw three kinds of friendship: for usefulness, for pleasure, and for character. The first two fade when the use or the fun ends. Only the third lasts, because each friend loves who the other is. Such a friend, he says, is "another self", and good friends make each other better. He thought nobody would choose a life without friends, even with everything else.

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** For Epicurus, friendship was the greatest help to a happy life, worth more than wealth or power. He lived it: his school, the Garden, was a community of friends outside politics, who shared meals and celebrations, and it welcomed women as students.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Friends help each other grow in virtue. A good friend tells you honestly when you are wrong, and does it with tact. But if the friend will not listen, you stop, rather than lose the friendship.

**Montaigne (Humanists and Essayists).** After his friend Étienne de La Boétie died young, Montaigne wrote that true friendship cannot be explained: it happens between these two people, and no others. He believed such a friendship is so complete that a person can have only one, and that it is very rare. In the same essay he says women had never reached this kind of friendship, a view common among writers of his time.

**Mencius (Confucianism).** Kindness, for Mencius, is in everyone from the start. Anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and distress, he said, without thinking of reward. That feeling of compassion is the seed of goodness, and it only needs to grow.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see friendship and kindness as among the best things in life, and link them to becoming a better person. They differ on numbers and reasons. Epicurus spoke openly of the safety and pleasure friends give; Aristotle cared most about friends valued for themselves; Montaigne thought the deepest kind happens only once. Nietzsche adds a sharper voice: a true friend should also challenge you.
sources: The app's thoughts #58, #112, #115, #117, #211, #280, #502, #503, #511, and #512, with their sources

pages.title: Habit and practice
sections: The question in one line
Are we what we repeatedly do?
How the traditions see it

**Epictetus and Aristotle (Stoicism, Classical Greek Philosophy).** If you want to be a good reader, said Epictetus, read; if a writer, write. Nothing great happens suddenly, not even a grape or a fig. Aristotle said the same of goodness: we become just by doing just acts.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Confucius compared learning to building a mound, one basket of earth at a time. If you stop one basket short, the stopping is your own doing; if you add one basket, you have moved forward. People start out much alike; practice sets them apart.

**The Dhammapada (Buddhist Philosophy).** The *Dhammapada* compares training the mind to a fletcher straightening an arrow. Small acts add up, like a water jar filling drop by drop, both for good and for bad. If you do something good, do it again, and take delight in it.

**Laozi and Zhuangzi (Taoism).** Every great thing starts small: the journey of a thousand li begins with a single step. Zhuangzi's cook has used the same knife for nineteen years. After long practice he no longer sees the whole ox, and works with his mind, following the natural gaps.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see small, repeated acts as the way a person changes. They differ on the goal. Confucius and Epictetus speak of steady effort; Zhuangzi's cook shows effort turning into ease. Kenkō and Hume add a warning: habits and customs also hold us, and few things are harder to give up.

pages.title: Happiness and the good life
sections: The question in one line
What does a good life need, and is happiness the point?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Happiness, for Aristotle, is the one thing we want for its own sake. His word, *eudaimonia*, means living well, or flourishing, not a passing mood. It is judged over a whole life: one swallow does not make a spring, and one good day does not make a happy life.

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** Epicurus made pleasure the goal, but not the pleasure of parties and luxury. He meant freedom from pain in the body and fear in the mind. Plain food, once hunger is gone, gives as much pleasure as a feast, and friends are the greatest help of all.

**Confucius and the Dhammapada (Confucianism, Buddhist Philosophy).** Both find happiness in contentment. Confucius said he could still find joy with coarse rice, water, and his bent arm for a pillow. For the *Dhammapada*, health is the greatest gift and contentment the best riches.

**Mill and Kant (Enlightenment Ethics).** Mill believed happiness is the goal, but some pleasures are higher than others: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. He also warned that happiness comes best on the side, while aiming at something else. Kant answered that morality is not about how to be happy, but how to become worthy of happiness.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most agree that happiness is not pleasure piled up, and that wanting less helps. They disagree on whether happiness is the aim of life. For Aristotle, Epicurus, and Mill it is, in different forms; for Kant, doing right comes first, whatever it costs.

pages.title: Justice
sections: The question in one line
What do we owe each other, and who decides?
How the traditions see it

**Plato and Socrates (Classical Greek Philosophy).** In Plato's *Republic*, a character called Thrasymachus says justice is simply what serves the strong. Plato's answer is that justice is a kind of harmony: each part of a person, or of a city, doing its proper job. His teacher Socrates went further. He said it is better to suffer an injustice than to do one, and that we should never return harm for harm.

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** For Aristotle, justice means giving people what they deserve, and good laws are reason without passion. A citizen is someone who takes turns ruling and being ruled. Yet the same book, the *Politics*, argues that some people are slaves by nature. Centuries later, this idea was used to defend the enslavement of Native Americans.

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** Epicurus saw no justice written into nature. For him, justice is an agreement between people not to harm each other, and it can change from place to place. It still matters to the individual: the just person lives with the most peace of mind.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Justice begins with the people who lead. A ruler who acts rightly will be followed without needing many orders. When someone wrongs you, answer with justice, not with kindness or revenge. In classical Confucian thought, justice was a personal and public virtue, not a matter of law or equal rights.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most agree that justice is about more than rules: it shapes the kind of person you become. They split on where it comes from. For Plato it is part of how things should be; for Epicurus, and later for social contract thinkers like Rousseau, it is something people agree on. Modern debates add new questions the ancients rarely asked, such as how fair inequality can be, as in John Rawls's "veil of ignorance", or whether punishment should aim to repair harm.
sources: "Plato's Ethics and Politics in The Republic"

pages.title: Karma and dharma
sections: The question in one line
Do our actions shape who we become, and is there a right path for each of us?
How the traditions see it

**The Upanishads (Indian Philosophy).** *Karma* simply means "action". In the older Vedic religion, it meant ritual acts that could earn a place in heaven. The Upanishads made it inward. In one of them, a person is made of desires: as we desire, so we will, and as we will, so we act. What we do, in turn, shapes what we become, in this life and the next.

**The Bhagavad Gita (Indian Philosophy).** *Dharma* comes from a root meaning "to hold" or "to support": the order that holds life together, and the right way to live within it. The Gita adds *svadharma*, your own dharma, and says it is better to follow your own path, even badly, than someone else's well. Its answer to karma is to act fully, but without craving the results. *Yoga*, in the Gita, is that discipline of action.

**The Buddhist texts (Buddhist Philosophy).** The Buddha moved karma from the act to the mind behind it: "Intention, I tell you, is karma." It is not fate: past actions shape what happens to us, but not how we respond. In Buddhism, *Dhamma* (the Pali form of dharma) also means something else: the Buddha's teaching itself, and the truth it points to. When the *Dhammapada* speaks of "the law", this is what it means.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Both traditions agree that actions have consequences that reach beyond the moment, and that what we do slowly makes us who we are. They part on the self: the Upanishads have a lasting self that carries its karma, while Buddhism has no permanent self at all. There is also an uncomfortable side. In Hindu law, each person's own dharma was tied to their class and station in life. Early Buddhist texts pushed back: "Not by birth is one a brahmin or an outcaste, but by deeds."

pages.title: Law and rights
sections: The question in one line
Where do laws get their authority, and what rights do we have?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Is it better to be ruled by the best person or the best laws? Aristotle leaned towards laws, because even good rulers have passions that bend their judgement. The law, he said, is reason unaffected by desire. Without law and justice, the human being is the worst of animals.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Confucius trusted example more than rules. To govern means to correct, and a ruler who acts rightly is followed without giving orders. When wronged, repay injury with justice, and kindness with kindness.

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** Epicurus saw no justice written into nature. Justice is an agreement between people not to harm each other or be harmed, and it can differ from place to place and time to time.

**Locke, Rousseau, and Wollstonecraft (Enlightenment Ethics).** Locke argued that all people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that good law does not shrink freedom but protects and enlarges it. Rousseau wanted laws the people make together, and warned that a state is lost once citizens stop caring. Wollstonecraft demanded that rights include women.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most of them see good law as a defence against the passions of the powerful; Sa'di put it simply: a tyrant cannot govern, for no one expects the shepherd's duty from the wolf. They split on where law comes from. For Aristotle and Locke, it rests on reason and nature; for Epicurus, on agreement; for Confucius, it matters less than the ruler's character.

pages.title: Learning and knowledge
sections: The question in one line
What is worth knowing, and how do we know that we know it?
How the traditions see it

**Socrates and Plato (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Socrates claimed one kind of wisdom: he did not think he knew what he didn't. He questioned people until they saw the limits of their own knowledge, which made him many enemies. For Plato, philosophy begins in wonder, and most of us are like prisoners in a cave, taking shadows for the real thing.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** Confucius loved learning and said it should never stop. Learning without thinking is wasted, and thinking without learning is dangerous. Real knowledge means saying what you know and admitting what you don't. Anyone can teach you something: copy the good in people, and correct in yourself the bad you see in them.

**Laozi and Zhuangzi (Taoism).** The Taoists doubted that more knowledge brings more wisdom. Learning adds something every day, but the Way is found by letting go, day by day. Zhuangzi adds that you cannot explain the ocean to a frog in a well: we all see from a narrow place.

**Hume and Mill (Enlightenment Ethics).** Hume asked for less certainty and more evidence: a wise person matches belief to the evidence. Mill added that you only half know your own view if you have never heard the other side. Even a true belief, never challenged, turns into dead dogma.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Nearly all of them start with humility: Socrates, Confucius, and Laozi all praise knowing the limits of what you know. They part ways on what to do next. Confucius and Mill say study and argue more; Laozi says empty your mind; Hume says follow the evidence and stay modest about the rest.

pages.title: Love
sections: The question in one line
What is love, and what does it ask of us?
How the traditions see it

**Plato (Classical Greek Philosophy).** In Plato's *Symposium*, guests at a dinner take turns praising love. One tells a myth: humans were once whole beings, cut in two, and love is the desire and pursuit of that lost whole. Then Socrates, quoting his teacher Diotima, describes love as a journey from one beautiful body towards ever purer beauty.

**Rumi, Hafiz, and Ibn Arabi (Persian and Sufi Poetry).** For the Sufi poets, human love and love of God mirror each other. Love hurts, and the pain is the proof of it. Hafiz admits he thought love would be easy, then found it a hard road. Ibn Arabi wrote that a heart grown in love can take on every form.

**Tagore and the Dhammapada (Indian Philosophy, Buddhist Philosophy).** Tagore saw love as the way we truly live in the world: when a person loves, giving becomes a joy, like a tree letting go of ripe fruit. The *Dhammapada* gives love a harder task: hatred never ends through hatred, only through love.

**Dostoevsky (Existential Thought).** Dostoevsky saw how easy it is to love in theory. Love in action, says a monk in *The Brothers Karamazov*, is harsh and dreadful compared with love in dreams. The same monk tells of a doctor who found that the more he loved humanity in general, the less he loved people in particular.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see love as more than a feeling: it changes the one who loves. They differ on its object. Plato and the Sufi poets point beyond the person towards something higher; Dostoevsky and Montaigne bring it back to one real person, loved, as Montaigne said of his friend, "because it was he, because it was I".
sources: The app's thoughts #106, #219, #221, #280, #308, #378, #389, #559, #567, and #577, with their sources

pages.title: Mind and emotions
sections: The question in one line
Should we master our feelings, or listen to them?
How the traditions see it

**Marcus Aurelius (Stoicism).** For the Stoics, what upsets us is not the event but our judgement about it, and we can learn to judge differently. Marcus Aurelius notes that the mind takes on the colour of its habitual thoughts. The ideal Stoic is free of disturbing passions, though not of all feeling.

**The Dhammapada (Buddhist Philosophy).** The *Dhammapada* opens with the claim that all we are comes from our thoughts. The mind is flighty and hard to hold, and taming it is the greatest good. Hatred never ends hatred; only love does.

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Aristotle did not want feelings gone, but right. Anyone can get angry. The skill is to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, and for the right reason. A good character is one that feels the right amount.

**Spinoza and Hume (Enlightenment Ethics).** Spinoza called being ruled by our emotions a kind of bondage, and said an emotion loses its grip once we understand it clearly. Hume turned the question around: reason on its own moves no one to act, and is, in his words, "the slave of the passions".
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most of them believe the mind can be trained, and that much suffering comes from how we react. They disagree on the goal. The Stoics and the Buddhist texts aim to calm or uproot troubling passions; Aristotle wants feelings in the right measure; Hume, like Pascal with his "heart" that has its own reasons, gives feeling the leading role.

pages.title: Nature and the universe
sections: The question in one line
What is the world made of, and where do we fit in it?
How the traditions see it

**Laozi and Zhuangzi (Taoism).** The Tao, the way of nature, cannot be fully named or explained. Its best image is water, which helps everything, takes the lowest place, and still wears away the hardest stone. A person lives well by following that way, not by forcing it.

**Lucretius and Epicurus (Epicureanism).** For the Epicureans, everything is made of atoms moving in empty space; worlds form by chance, without any need for gods. Lucretius wrote that fear comes from not knowing the causes of things. Understanding nature, he said, is the cure for that fear.

**Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus (Stoicism).** The Stoics saw the opposite: one living whole, shaped by reason, in which every part is connected. Marcus Aurelius told himself to see the universe as a single being with one substance and one soul. Epictetus reminded his students how small a part of it each of us is.

**Kant and Pascal (Enlightenment Ethics, Existential Thought).** Two things filled Kant with ever-growing awe: the starry heavens above and the moral law within. Pascal saw human beings as reeds, the weakest thing in nature, but reeds that think, and our greatness lies in that thought.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them say that understanding nature changes how we live in it. They split on whether it has a purpose. The Stoics see a rational order; the Epicureans see atoms and chance; the Taoists see a way that cannot be put into words. The Japanese writers add something simpler: notice it, from the dawn to the flowers.

pages.title: Purpose and meaning
sections: The question in one line
What is a life for?
How the traditions see it

**Aristotle (Classical Greek Philosophy).** Aristotle noticed that everything we do aims at some good, and those goods point to a final one: happiness, the thing we want for its own sake. For him, the question of meaning had an answer: a life of reason and virtue, lived well.

**Tolstoy and William James (Existential Thought).** Tolstoy had fame, family, and wealth when his life "came to a standstill": he could no longer see what any of it was for. William James answered the same fear in a lecture called "Is Life Worth Living?". We live fully, he said, only by risking ourselves on what we believe.

**Mill (Enlightenment Ethics).** At twenty, Mill asked himself whether reaching all his goals would make him happy, and an honest voice said no. He came out of the crisis with a lesson: happiness comes to those who aim at something other than their own happiness.

**George Eliot, Dickinson, and Tagore (Humanists and Essayists, Indian Philosophy).** Many find meaning in what we do for others. "What do we live for," asks a character in *Middlemarch*, "if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?" Dickinson would not live in vain if she could stop one heart from breaking, and Tagore says we earn our life by giving it.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most of them say meaning comes from something larger than the self, whether virtue, a cause, or other people. They differ on whether it is given or made. Aristotle finds it in human nature; Nietzsche says you must become what you are; Zhuangzi gently mocks the whole idea, praising a useless tree that lives long because nobody wants it.

pages.title: Self-knowledge
sections: The question in one line
Who are you, really, and can you ever know?
How the traditions see it

**Socrates (Classical Greek Philosophy).** At his trial, Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living. For him, questioning yourself and others was not a hobby but a duty, worth dying for.

**The Upanishads and the Buddhist texts (Indian Philosophy, Buddhist Philosophy).** The Upanishads look for a deep, lasting Self behind body and mind, and find it one with the Self in all beings. Buddhism turns this around. In *The Questions of King Milinda*, a chariot is just a name for its parts working together, and so is a person: there is no fixed self to find.

**Confucius (Confucianism).** For Confucius, self-knowledge is daily practice. One of his students examined himself every day on three points: had he been loyal, been true to his friends, and practised what he was taught? The superior man looks for the cause of things in himself; the petty man looks for it in others.

**Montaigne and La Rochefoucauld (Humanists and Essayists).** Montaigne made himself the subject of his *Essays*, because each person carries the whole human condition. La Rochefoucauld was less hopeful: we are so used to wearing masks for others that in the end we are disguised to ourselves.
Where they agree, and where they don't

They all say the work begins inside, not in other people's opinions. They differ on what you find there: a lasting Self (the Upanishads), no fixed self at all (Buddhism), a self you still have to create (Nietzsche's "become what you are"), or a mirror of everyone (Montaigne).

pages.title: Solitude and stillness
sections: The question in one line
Why is it so hard to sit still, and what do we find when we do?
How the traditions see it

**Pascal (Existential Thought).** Pascal thought all human misfortune comes from one thing: we cannot stay quietly in a room. We chase distraction to avoid thinking about ourselves, and that distraction is itself our greatest misery.

**Marcus Aurelius (Stoicism).** While ruling an empire, Marcus longed for a house in the country or by the sea, as rich Romans had. Then he reminded himself that he could retreat into his own mind whenever he chose, and that there is no quieter place.

**Laozi and Zhuangzi (Taoism).** Muddy water, says the *Tao Te Ching*, becomes clear if you let it be still. Zhuangzi says the wise use the mind like a mirror: it grasps nothing and refuses nothing, and reflects what comes without holding on.

**Kenkō and Chōmei (Japanese Aesthetics).** The Japanese recluses praised a quiet life away from the crowd. Kenkō asked how anyone could find leisure tiresome: free from cares, it is good simply to be alone. From his small hut, Chōmei watched the moon at his window and thought of people of old.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see stillness as the place where the mind clears. They differ on how alone to be. Schopenhauer and Nietzsche praise solitude itself, and the *Dhammapada* says it is better to travel alone than with a fool. For Marcus, though, the retreat is inward and can be taken anywhere, even in the middle of public life.

pages.title: Suffering and resilience
sections: The question in one line
What do we do with pain we cannot avoid?
How the traditions see it

**Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, and Boethius (Stoicism).** Marcus Aurelius asked to be like a headland that the waves keep breaking on, while it stands firm. Epictetus advised wishing for things to happen as they do, not as we would like. In prison, Boethius wrote that nothing is wretched unless we think it so.

**Rumi and Hafiz (Persian and Sufi Poetry).** The Sufi poets see pain as part of the way. Rumi calls it a treasure that holds mercies, and the *Masnavi* opens with a reed flute crying for the reed bed it was cut from. Hafiz says no one reaches joy without passing through hardship.

**Nietzsche and Dostoevsky (Existential Thought).** Nietzsche's answer was *amor fati*, love of fate: wanting nothing to be different, the hard parts included. Dostoevsky went further, calling suffering the origin of consciousness itself.

**Weil and Mill (Existential Thought, Enlightenment Ethics).** Others look outward. Simone Weil said those who suffer need, above all, people able to pay them attention. And Mill believed most of the great causes of suffering can be reduced by human care and effort.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Many of them say suffering can teach and deepen us, as Vivekananda put it: misery is sometimes a greater teacher than happiness. They differ on where the answer lies. The Stoics look to our own judgement, the Sufi poets to love and longing, Weil to other people, and Mill to changing the world itself.

pages.title: The self and the soul
sections: The question in one line
Is there a lasting "you" behind your body, your thoughts, and your moods?
How the traditions see it

**The Upanishads (Indian Philosophy).** The Upanishads look for the *Atman*, the deepest self, behind body and mind. It is what makes all the other faculties work. Their boldest claim is that this inner self is one with *Brahman*, the reality behind the whole universe. The Katha Upanishad pictures it as a traveller sitting in a chariot: the body is the chariot, and the intellect holds the reins.

**The Buddhist texts (Buddhist Philosophy).** Buddhism turned this around. Its teaching of *anatta*, "not-self", says there is no permanent soul at all. A person is made of five changing parts: body, feelings, perceptions, impulses, and consciousness. In *The Questions of King Milinda*, the monk Nagasena uses the same image of a chariot: it is only a name for its parts working together, and so is a person.

**Plato (Classical Greek Philosophy).** For Plato, the soul is the true self. It is not made of matter, and it does not die with the body. In the *Phaedrus* he uses a chariot too: reason is the driver, pulled by two horses, one noble and one ruled by appetite. A good life is a driver who keeps both in hand.

**Al-Ghazali and the Sufis (Persian and Sufi Poetry).** In Islam the word *nafs* means self, but for the Sufis it is above all the lower self, the ego with its pride and cravings. The Quran names three stages: the self that urges us to do wrong, the self that blames itself, and the self at peace. Al-Ghazali compared the body to a horse and the soul to its rider, and called the struggle with the lower self the greatest struggle of all.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Three of these traditions reach for the same picture, a chariot, which says something about the question: who, if anyone, is holding the reins? The Upanishads and Plato answer with a lasting self that outlives the body. The Buddhist texts answer that there is no one there to find, a view Hume reached by another road when he called the self a bundle of perceptions. The Sufis care less about what the self is than about what to do with it. And Epicurus disagreed with almost everyone: for him, the soul ends with the body, so death is nothing to fear.

pages.title: Time and the present
sections: The question in one line
Is life short, or do we waste it?
How the traditions see it

**Seneca (Stoicism).** Seneca argued that life is not short; we make it short by wasting it. How late, he said, to begin living just when we must leave. Epictetus added that he wanted to be present like the hour, and to pass like the hour.

**Epicurus (Epicureanism).** Epicurus warned against putting off joy for a tomorrow we do not control. The future is neither fully ours nor fully out of our hands. And remembering the good days we have had is part of a happy life.

**Omar Khayyam and Hafiz (Persian and Sufi Poetry).** The Persian poets feel time slipping past. Khayyam's "Moving Finger" writes and moves on, and nothing can make it go back. Their answer is to make the most of the days we have.

**Kenkō and Pascal (Japanese Aesthetics, Existential Thought).** Kenkō noted that the seasons come in order, but death comes when it likes, so we should not put off what matters. Pascal saw the same habit from another side: we never live, but only hope to live.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them say the present is the only time we truly have. They differ on what to fill it with: pleasure and wine for Khayyam, wisdom and duty for Seneca, quiet attention for Kenkō. Montaigne sums up the common ground: life is measured by its use, not its length.

pages.title: Tolerance
sections: The question in one line
How do we live with people who believe differently?
How the traditions see it

**Locke (Enlightenment Ethics).** In *A Letter Concerning Toleration* (1689), Locke argued that faith cannot be forced, so the state should not try. Churches are voluntary groups, and religion is a matter for each person. But his tolerance had limits: he refused it to atheists, whose promises he thought could not be trusted, and to churches whose members owed loyalty to a foreign ruler.

**Voltaire (Enlightenment Ethics).** After a Protestant merchant, Jean Calas, was executed in Toulouse in 1762 on a false charge, Voltaire wrote his *Treatise on Tolerance*. In his *Philosophical Dictionary* he calls tolerance the mark of our humanity: we are all made of weakness and error, so let us forgive each other's foolishness. Prejudice, he adds, is an opinion without judgement, taught to children before they can think.

**Mill (Enlightenment Ethics).** Mill moved the question from religion to every kind of opinion. If all of humanity but one person agreed, they would have no more right to silence that person than the one would have to silence them. Silencing a view, he said, assumes we cannot be wrong.

**Ibn Arabi and Okakura (Persian and Sufi Poetry, Japanese Aesthetics).** Ibn Arabi wrote of a heart that can take on every form: a monastery, a temple, a place of pilgrimage. Okakura, writing in English for Western readers, said East and West had grown along different lines, with no reason why one should not complete the other.
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them see that forcing belief does not work and that our own views may be wrong. They disagree on the limits. Locke still excluded some groups; Voltaire mostly had religious violence in mind; Mill defended almost any opinion, short of harm to others.

pages.title: War and peace
sections: The question in one line
Can war ever be right, and what makes peace last?
How the traditions see it

**Laozi and the Dhammapada (Taoism, Buddhist Philosophy).** The *Tao Te Ching* says the most skilled warrior shows no warlike look and never gives way to rage. The *Dhammapada* sees what victory costs: it breeds hatred, because the loser is unhappy. And the greatest victory is over yourself, not over a thousand armies.

**The Bhagavad Gita (Indian Philosophy).** The *Gita* is set on a battlefield. Prince Arjuna sees relatives, friends, and teachers in the enemy ranks, drops his bow, and refuses to fight. Krishna urges him to do his duty as a warrior. Yet Gandhi learned the last verses of its second chapter by heart and kept them as a companion in his non-violent movement.

**Hobbes and Kant (Enlightenment Ethics).** Hobbes, who lived through civil war, described life without government as a war of all against all. Peace, for him, needs a strong ruler; a commonwealth, he wrote, is the mother of peace. Kant hoped for more: in *Towards Perpetual Peace* (1795) he proposed republics joined in a union of states.

**Voltaire and Tolstoy (Enlightenment Ethics, Existential Thought).** Voltaire noted a sad truth: wishing your country to be great usually means wishing harm on your neighbours. Tolstoy went furthest: read literally, he said, the Sermon on the Mount forbids resisting evil by force. His ideas on non-violence deeply impressed Gandhi.
Where they agree, and where they don't

None of them see war as glorious in itself. They split on whether it can be justified. The *Gita* accepts a just duty to fight, and Hobbes and Kant seek peace through political order; Tolstoy rejects violence altogether. Sa'di adds a quieter thought: a falsehood that brings peace can be better than a truth that stirs up harm.

pages.title: Work and action
sections: The question in one line
How should we act, and what should we expect from it?
How the traditions see it

**The Bhagavad Gita and Vivekananda (Indian Philosophy).** In the *Gita*, Krishna tells Arjuna that his business is with the action alone, never with its fruits. It is better to do your own task imperfectly than someone else's well. Vivekananda put it simply: work without stopping, but without attachment.

**Marcus Aurelius (Stoicism).** Even an emperor found it hard to get up in the morning. His reminder to himself: I am rising to do the work of a human being. He also told himself to stop talking about what a good man should be, and simply be one.

**Laozi and Zhuangzi (Taoism).** The Taoists value action that does not force. Governing a great state, says the *Tao Te Ching*, is like cooking small fish: stir too much and they fall apart. Zhuangzi's cook works with the grain of things, and his knife stays sharp for nineteen years.

**Confucius and Voltaire (Confucianism, Enlightenment Ethics).** Confucius praised the person who acts first and speaks afterwards. At the end of Voltaire's *Candide*, after war, shipwreck, and earthquake, the hero stops arguing about whether all is for the best. "We must cultivate our garden."
Where they agree, and where they don't

All of them trust deeds over words. They differ on effort and reward. The *Gita* and the Stoics speak of duty done well whatever the result; the Taoists warn against forcing things; Voltaire suggests that useful work close to home may be the best answer to questions we cannot solve.

pages.title: Work and wealth
sections: The question in one line
How much is enough, and what is work for?
How the traditions see it

**Epicurus and Marcus Aurelius (Epicureanism, Stoicism).** Epicurus said nature's wealth is limited and easy to get, while the wealth of empty wishes has no end. Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, reminded himself each morning that he was rising to do the work of a human being.

**Confucius and Sa'di (Confucianism, Persian and Sufi Poetry).** Confucius could find joy with coarse rice and water, and called riches gained by wrongdoing a floating cloud. Being poor without complaining is hard, he said; being rich without pride is easy. Sa'di advised anyone who wants riches to ask for contentment instead.

**Adam Smith and Rousseau (Enlightenment Ethics).** Adam Smith argued in *The Wealth of Nations* that wealth grows through free exchange and the division of labour, as if guided by an "invisible hand". Yet his first book began with sympathy: however selfish we are, we care about others' happiness. Rousseau saw a darker side: the first person who fenced off land, said "This is mine", and found people simple enough to believe it, opened the way to crimes, wars, and misery.

**Vivekananda and Schopenhauer (Indian Philosophy, Existential Thought).** Vivekananda taught that the best work is done for no reward, neither money nor fame. Schopenhauer compared riches to sea water: the more you drink, the thirstier you get.
Where they agree, and where they don't

Most of them warn that wealth beyond need rarely brings peace. They differ on what wealth does for society. Smith saw trade and work as the way whole nations grow richer; Rousseau saw property as the root of inequality; the Stoics and the *Gita* tradition care less about the wealth than about the spirit in which we work.
